speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In accordance with the decision of this House to have a simultaneous debate on both Motions, I will now call on Members to make their speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are allowed to consider both Motions in a single speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you do have any clarifications for either mover of the Motion, you can weave it into your speech.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Minister Indranee shared with us on 4 October 2022 in response to my Parliamentary Question (PQ), many couples continue to aspire to have their own home before they start a family.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The affordability and accessibility of HDB flats therefore play a very important role in our TFR.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) contends that our current housing policies has delivered on either affordability or accessibility, but not both.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: New flats are affordable after grants and subsidies, but not accessible due to the long waiting time.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Resale flats are accessible but not affordable due to high resale prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the reality and predicament faced by young Singaporeans when they are looking at getting married and starting a family.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us look at these issues one by one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND) tracks waiting time by measuring time from the point of successful Build-To-Order (BTO) booking to the point of key collection.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This waiting time does not include time spent on unsuccessful applications.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for young couples, the waiting time for HDB flats starts from their very first application, whether successful or not.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is some disparity in the concept of waiting time between the two groups.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As MND does not track the time from first application to key collection, it makes it difficult to grasp how long couples have to wait from the time they decide to get married to each other to the time they get the keys to their first flat.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All we have are anecdotes here and there, which build up the impression that our young people mostly feel that the waiting times for BTOs are too long.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been evident for a while that the BTO approach is not meeting the needs of young Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's launch of a small number of flats with a Shorter Waiting Time (SWT) is recognition of this.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a small proportion of the total supply of new flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under SWT, flats are constructed in advance before they are launched for booking.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is already a departure from the BTO approach.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time to face up to the fact that the BTO approach is not satisfactory and to start to build for projected demand based on factors like marriage rate and new citizens growth rate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has the means to forecast and project.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was a lesson in the past for over-building but that should not stop us from exploring options to be proactive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Former Minister Mah Bow Tan changed from the Registration for Flats system to a BTO system because the registration queue fluctuated widely in the wake of the 1997 Financial Crisis.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We agree that a registration queue that required no commitment is an unreliable indicator.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, annual marriage and new citizen numbers are relatively stable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of new citizens each year is about 20,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, there is always a demand for rental flats to provide the buffer for any excess flats built.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the meantime, efforts need to be made to accelerate building to clear the current backlog and shorten the waiting times for current and future cohorts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is an average of 20,000 units per year from 2021 to 2025.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This supply of flats pales in comparison to the past.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is an average of 37,900 units per year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister explain why HDB is not supplying more flats when it is possible to do so?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister said in his National Day Rally speech that "our problem is not finding the space to build enough flats".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, if land is not the constraint, what is causing us to be unable to build as fast as 40 years ago, despite technological advancements?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the saying goes, when there is a will, there is a way.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Government lack the political will to tackle the low TFR problem we are facing?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our low TFR has resulted in our over-reliance on foreign manpower, which has brought along a whole suite of other issues, like job competition, social friction and national identity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I will not go into these issues today.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Increasing the supply of new flats would not only shorten the waiting time for future applicants, enable them to get married and start a family earlier, it would also spur economic growth at a time when global growth is slowing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP therefore urges the Government to increase the supply of new flats in the immediate term.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MND has placed a full-page advertisement in The Straits Times with examples of different couples at different income levels paying for flats of different sizes to illustrate the affordability of new flats after Government subsidies and grants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These examples illustrate how different couples are able to pay for their flats using only their CPF, with no cash payment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is not illustrated is what happens to retirement adequacy after paying for the flats using CPF.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the other income groups, close to two-thirds or more are used up.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This adversely affects the adequacy of their retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This payout is not enough to meet expenses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Researchers at LKYSPP and NTU conducted a study in 2017 to 2018 and estimated that the amount required is about $1,379 per month.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With inflation, this amount must now be higher.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what about the one-third who cannot even meet the Basic Retirement Sum?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At worst, retirees are unable to meet basic expenses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At best, retirees suffer a lower standard of living after retirement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: New HDB flats used to be even more affordable, under the previous generation of PAP leaders.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the prices of new HDB flats have been rising over the years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two ways to achieve this: one, stretch the loan repayment over a longer period of time so that each instalment is lower and hence affordable; two, by giving Government subsidies and grants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first method worsens retirement adequacy because it means that CPF money is being drained for a longer period of time and the amount of interest to be paid also increases significantly with a longer loan tenure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second method provides an illusion of affordability by presenting a selling price after subsidies and grants that is lower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But where do the Government subsidies and grants come from?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From taxpayers, from the GST that we pay, from incomes taxes, from duties on liquor and tobacco, taxes on petrol and vehicles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, while the Government subsidies and grants are not paid directly by the flat buyers, we are all indirectly paying for everybody's HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the Government grants can create a price spiral.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As grants are also provided for resale flats, this increases the purchasing power of the buyers, hence increasing demand and therefore, resale prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When resale prices increase, to help first timers afford resale flats, grants will have to be increased, thus leading to a price spiral.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Meanwhile, when resale prices increase, the Chief Valuer looks at recent transactions and revises land prices upwards.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means HDB needs to pay more to the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) to be put into the reserves and the price of new flats before subsidies increases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the price of new flats before subsidy increases, either more tax revenue is needed to provide more subsidies and grants or flat buyers must pay more.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Either way, the amount paid into the reserves continues to grow larger and larger as resale prices increase, paid for by flat buyers and taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In summary, the affordability comes at the expense of retirement savings and taxpayers who have to fund the Government subsidies and grants for HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP is therefore proposing a different pricing model for affordable housing as mentioned by my colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this model, new flats are sold to Singaporeans without collecting the land price upfront.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if the flat is subsequently sold by the original buyers, the land cost will then be recovered from the resale price.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the land cost is taken out, the upfront payment will be significantly lower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the biggest problems in any attempts to offer new flats at lower prices is the uncertainty over the effect on resale prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, under this proposal, since land cost must be paid at the point of resale, this puts the new flats on par with the other flats sold earlier with land cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will serve to preserve the value of existing flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another problem we are currently facing is the lease decay issue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the remaining lease of an HDB flat gets shorter, the value of the flat drops.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the end of 99 years, the flat returns to the Government and the value thus goes to zero.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The worry is that flat buyers who used most of their CPF funds to buy the flat will be left with little retirement funds as the value of their flats goes to zero.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under this proposal, with the land cost deferred, the amount of CPF withdrawn to pay for the flat will be much lower, leaving Singaporeans with more funds in their CPF.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will make the lease decay less of a problem.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I wish to touch on HDB flats for singles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, we propose that singles be allowed to buy 3-room flats or smaller.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singles who own a 3-room flat will be able to get married immediately upon finding a suitable partner and even have children whilst applying for a bigger flat.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let HDB flats not be the reason for any delays in marriage and having children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our low TFR is not only affecting our economy, it is also affecting the make-up of our social fabric, the social support for the elderly and our national defence.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has been such a long-standing problem and with the feedback that our young want their own homes before starting a family, why are we not taking decisive steps to address this?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister mentioned that if we do not charge land at market prices, that will lead to a reduction in the value of the reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Minister agree that it would be unfair if we are comparing public housing with private properties and leasehold properties with freehold properties?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The topic of housing is thus not new and one that is close to many people's hearts as it touches their daily lives and is one that they cannot do without.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is also a complex topic as it ranges from ownership, subsidies, land value needs, flat types, location, people's lifestyles to the norms within a society and across generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In 2018, I spoke at length in this House about public housing as it was a top concern for a majority of Singaporeans who were concerned about housing affordability and choice as well as capital and retirement value.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Back then, a key concern was on homeowners of older HDB flats who were worried about the value of their homes as their leases shortened, compounded by a lacklustre resale market that had persisted for six consecutive quarters.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, my Ministry of National Development (MND) colleagues and I will be touching on various aspects of housing that concerns Singaporeans and making suggestions for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I will focus on the notion of home accessibility and affordability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To look at affordability and accessibility of homes in Singapore, let us begin from the fundamental of public housing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When public housing was first introduced in Singapore, it was with the intent of providing homes to every citizen and enabling those living in the kampungs who had to make way for land development to have a place to live in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The flats built in the late-1970s to early-1980s housed many of those in the generations before us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my view, what has changed most is the demand pattern and the lifestyles of the subsequent generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All these have an impact on the affordability and the accessibility of homes currently and into the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, people over time do not live in their first public flat for more than two to three decades, unlike those of my grandparents' generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When the younger generation gains independence, be they single or married, they would like to have a place of their own and live separately from their parents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, amongst this group, there are still many whom we know who wish to live near their parents or extended family in order to have support for the caregiving of their children or for them to take care of their parents conveniently.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I see this in my own 	Fengshan constituency as it is a mature estate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many families have three generations living near one other, within walking distance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The challenge with the ease of finding a home in the same estate is difficult as there is limited or no new land, in fact, for new flats to be built within the vicinity of the existing flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What this means is that their children will naturally have to purchase the nearest BTO flats around Bedok Town, failing which are other new public housing projects in the East or settling for resale flats in the same vicinity or for some even purchasing from private housing nearby.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In mature estates where there are ready amenities and access to public transportation, actually quite contrary to what PSP has said, I think that we have seen that the housing located in such places have inevitably risen in prices over time even when the lease diminishes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, let us look at the price of a public flat versus a condominium for the mass market in a mature estate with a 99-year lease.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The affordability of a flat is more than just the final price of the purchased flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It also includes the value of maintaining the flat and the value of the flat when it is ready for resale in the market.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All these years, HDB has continued to maintain and upkeep the public flats through Town Council works.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It also provides subventions for the upkeeping of major infrastructures like lifts, common amenities like linkways, community gardens, playgrounds, exercise corners and much more.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: HDB also continues to provide schemes like lift upgrading, home improvement programmes, neighbourhood renewal programmes – I know this more because in Fengshan, we have had all these programmes, except, the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) in future, to ensure the flats remain liveable and safe.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All these help in the general capital appreciation of the flats, having residents to pay very little of their own money for operations of these facilities and any new additions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In sharp contrast, unlike public housing, in private housing like condominiums, all these infrastructure maintenance, upgrades and new builds have to be paid through the sinking fund collections from every household within that condominium.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If the condominium does not have sufficient sinking funds, they will be unable to carry out any additional or amendment works.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While most people understand the concept and the differences between having a public flat and a private condominium, the feeling of ownership of a 99-year lease property of a HDB versus a private apartment is not quite the same.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: On a comparable basis, one can conclude that the relative cost of a similar size and the same leasehold public flat versus that of a private apartment already significantly differs starting from the purchase price, its maintenance over time, the continual upgrading and the rate of capital value appreciation at resale – unless the private condominium has an en-bloc opportunity.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Third, I believe that no single approach for a complex topic like housing will be effective on its own.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Any artificial intervention on the price of today's HDB flats based on a free-market model will have significant repercussions on our social fabric and the wealth of different generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Take some of my residents and those whom I know who purchased their HDB flats in the 1980s.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, many of them still live in the flats and they are still first-time owners.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Yet, many of them told me they wish to continue living in it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: They do not want to monetise even though they can get good monies for it at this point and it is attractive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: They do not want to sell the flat and downgrade to a shorter lease flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, I really wanted to ask the Member, Mr Leong Mun Wai, on his position when he said that there is a need to review our public housing policy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I do not think HDB stands still on this and does not review our public housing policy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But it is interesting when he said that we need to make a reset to it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Because my question would be related to, if in the short term, we need to make up for this delta of shortage of BTO flats, but to what Ms Hazel Poa actually said, that we have to continue building it in large volumes, like about 40 years ago.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What would really happen to all these flats, because we would have such a large number of them?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And knowing that we have a shrinking population and ageing population with low total fertility rate, can these owners in future still rely on their flat for retirement?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Will they be able to sell to anyone in the long run or would there even be buyers in the future?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think we need to look at the supply of flats from a few angles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, our supply of flats come from our BTO flats, our resale flats and also rental flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If we want the Government to intervene and also to make resale flats more affordable for the younger generation, this simply means we may have to do a few bold things.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And these, in my opinion, are bold things: one, to convince our parents and ourselves to settle for less profits when we sell our subsidised flats; two, be willing to live in the same property for a much longer time and not inflate the demand on a cyclical basis; three, to accept a new definition of living proximity to our parents or their extended family in estates that are non-mature and at distances beyond 15 kilometres of one another; four – and I think this is quite important – to not constantly ask for more subsidies in different forms because, if we are honest about it, we know this must be paid through taxes or other means.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While the above that I have mentioned will not completely resolve the concern of affordability, it will at least be a start to shifting the whole balance on housing supply and demand in a more calibrated manner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: After the supply shortage has been better addressed post-pandemic, what can be done for those buyers with genuine requirements for flats and first-timers particularly, who are purchasing flats after four attempts of BTO and/or Sale of Balance Flats (SBF).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, to review if the downsizing options for owners from private housing should be limited to some flat sizes unless they are above a particular age group.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Such high home ownership brings with it different challenges, especially when individuals or families are unable to obtain their first public flat after several attempts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It not only upsets people but also makes one think why others are always luckier than themselves when it comes to securing a flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To make matters worse, nobody actually feels good when they see others making a windfall from the sale of a subsidised HDB flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But at the end of the day, let us focus on the fundamental of why public housing was first established since this country’s Independence.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It was really to provide housing access and making it affordable for every citizen.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This Government and our forefathers have tried to ensure this basic objective is met.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have rescheduled two of you to tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Will there be any objection for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and the Workers’ Party (WP) Members to speak tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You have sent in your request, so I have made adjustments for two of them to speak tomorrow as indicated in my note to you.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The thing is, we have the Minister who has just given out nine annexes and we would like to respond more fully to the Minister's contributions and we understand that — unless of course, the debate on the Motion is going to be completed today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No, it will not be completed today, so we have to toggle some of the speakers from tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My request – and I am not going to be argumentative about this, but there are 23 speakers on the speakers list.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And there are four WP speakers on the Motion, my request is four —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, we will shift two of them to tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Would it be possible for all the WP speakers to speak tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It will not be against the Standing Orders.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No, I will shift two of them to tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In Sengkang, I have spoken to residents, even elderly ones, who own their own homes, who worry about how expensive buying a flat in Singapore is and fear especially for their children and their grandchildren this ability to continue affording a roof over their heads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Newspaper reports that point to a record high in property prices and rent in many housing districts reinforce this notion that housing is unaffordable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My contribution to this debate will focus on what is driving these high house prices, but I will end with some proposals for easing a transition as we seek a reset to some degree in house pricing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: HDB remains a success in public housing globally, producing what some regard to be the most admired public housing programme worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it has been rather less successful in some of its original goals, crucially in meeting terms of affordability and access.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My Workers' Party (WP) colleagues Leon Perera and Gerald Giam will in their speeches, elaborate more on these aspects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This has knock-on effects on our cost of living and crucially, our retirement savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The way the Government has tried to thread this needle has been to provide taxpayer subsidies, funded subsidies to young families trying to purchase their first home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Hence, Build-To-Order (BTO) and Sales of Balance Flats (SBF), and even resale purchases, enjoy a bevy of grants to help them get on the local property ladder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For many of these schemes, they may even get to enjoy two bites of the cherry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Once you are on the ladder, there is less worry that house prices might run away from you because when you sell your place, you receive the market price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And even if prices are too high, you at least have the cash from your sale to offset that hit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But what this approach does is that it uses tax revenue to offset the hit from the costly market pricing of public housing in an effort to preserve the affordability of HDB flats and enabling the asset enhancement aspect of public housing to remain in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It reassures those who have pumped a good part of their retirement savings into real estate that they will eventually be able to realise the investment gains from this decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Moreover, since most HDB homeowners use their CPF savings to pay for this mortgage, the status quo allows them to extract funds that would otherwise have been locked in their CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This preserves their monthly disposable income and also helps them to commit to saving for their retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But what this does is conflate two competing ideals: growing retirement assets as much as possible to ensure retirement adequacy while simultaneously keeping public housing as affordable as possible so Singaporeans have a roof over their heads that they may call home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In principle, any asset with a finite shelf-life should have a very clear path of future prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Every year, as we gradually approach the point in time, where it will eventually expires with no value, the price would drop by just a little bit because of the technicalities of how we value time, which is that we tend to value the present more than we do the future, you tend to see a smaller decline each year at the beginning, but as we stretch out further into the future, prices will drop by ever-greater increments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Members may also access this on the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In Singapore, the chart above is what policy-makers have enshrined as the so-called Bala's Curve, which law attributes to a land office employee with that name who first drew up this theoretical relationship for 99-year leasehold properties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The premise behind the curve is as elegant as it looks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The price of the house should be worth what you would otherwise pay in rent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If you buy, you are essentially front-loading your payments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, after you are done with your mortgage, you get to enjoy living rent-free in your home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But the valuation of your home is still whatever the accumulated sum of what you would otherwise be paying for in rent for the remainder of the time that the house is still yours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I will just ask all of you to cast your eyes to the other chart on the lower half of the page.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There, you will see essentially the same curve, but with one very mild variation – we allow inflation to enter into the picture so that it will affect what you pay in rent every year into the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: With this very simple tweak, we will see exactly what we observe in Singapore's housing market: a steadily rising house price which tops out somewhere around the two-thirds mark of the total lease.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is also incidentally what real estate agents often share about how they believe flat prices will move when leases are in the final three decades – that they are basically impossible to sell; and if they were, the prices would have to drop precipitously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This chart actually shows three lines which correspond to three different average inflation rates over the period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And what do these three lines correspond to?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first is inflation, ever since 1991, when the Government began adopting its asset enhancement approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second is what happens when we add in higher inflation for the post-pandemic period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just two years of above-average inflation was sufficient to trigger a significant increase in house prices at the peak relative to the business-as-usual scenario.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Higher rents eventually make their way into higher house prices and vice versa.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Given our recent brush with high inflation, it would be unsurprising that house prices have likewise breached new heights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This just means the need for even bigger taxpayer-funded grants from the Government if we wish to keep housing affordable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It also means that our current HDB and CPF policies may become a dangerous game of musical chairs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If one is able to offload one's flat before its price collapses, as it must eventually, then we can retire comfortably.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But then the one holding the bag is a fellow Singaporean – someone who bought your resale because they needed space for a growing family and could not afford to wait for a BTO.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Of course, some might argue that using the discounted value of rent to determine house prices is only one method and solely relying on this approach to explain high house prices could be misleading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There is at least one other common valuation approach and that is what some may call an adding up approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Basically, we add in the price of land, the construction costs and the developer's profits to arrive at a price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The unknown factor in this, of course, is what land should cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Minister for National Development recently explained this further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Minister Desmond Lee told us that land sale prices for private housing developments are not used but that "relevant public housing transactions" are used instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If this is true, then we have not truly unshackled ourselves from the possibility that the land component, even for BTOs, may be overvalued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What is worse – this bubble can feed on itself as the resale market cross-references the BTO one, back and forth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What is needed then is a way for us to price land not in reference to the market but in a way that we can justify via fundamentals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One approach is to peg this at historical acquisition prices or, as Mr Leong Mun Wai has suggested today, to value it but only to realise the cost after the land is sold for profit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Another way to do so is as a multiple of median salaries from new workers – a median the WP would prefer a multiple somewhat closer to three – but crucially, we should do this pre-emptively instead of as a target after market valuations have already been set.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Doing so would ensure that it is HDB that is driving affordability, not trying to catch up to a market with subsidies, so that the tail does not end up wagging the dog.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Let us first get some preliminary objections out of the way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A common refrain by this Government is simply following well-established market principles of land valuation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Should there be any deviation from this approach, it would amount to a raiding of the reserves since our land trust belongs not just to the current but also future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First off, this argument is, even by the Government's own accounting conventions, fundamentally incoherent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Singapore Land Authority (SLA) already exempts land leases of less than seven years from registration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) currently treats income from land lasting less than 10 years in lease as recurrent income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If it is true that carving out part of the lease amounts to raiding the reserves, then this Government has also done the same for every short-term land lease that it makes where the proceeds are credited as recurrent revenue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Furthermore, the Government already exercises differential land pricing for different classes and uses of land.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Land zones for private residential purposes are valued differently from those for commercial uses and also differently from land use for infrastructure such as roads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While I am not suggesting that HDB flats should be priced at some unreasonably low quantum, it is fair to ask why land for public housing does not better reflect its public nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But let us also be clear-eyed in what the trade-off we are making is about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, we are, in effect, asking the present generation to pay more to support future ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There is not really a single right answer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But let us at least acknowledge that it is not necessarily selfish or greedy or even lacking in foresight to want some of the benefits of our land trust to be realised today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, we all want the best for our children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Sometimes, that means leaving behind a sound inheritance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it also means providing for them today with a roof over their heads and the comforts of a home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It also means being present for them as they grow up and not constantly pulling long hours at work just so that we can afford the home that we are living in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: More generally, we should recognise that the market does not price everything perfectly and perhaps, more crucially, it does not price everything that is important in life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I know this sounds strange coming from an economist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In this case, when the market is able to price, even imperfectly, the value of land, it fails to price the value of the right to shelter and, in particular, the affordable shelter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A friend once liked to quip that, "price is what you pay but value is what you get".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Economists fully understand this, which is why we do not rely solely on the market to govern our lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, while it is probably true that it would be a step too far to price land at zero, it is also not unreasonable to say that we should value public land in a way that simultaneously reflects these intangible values.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: All we need, I believe, is a reboot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But if we were to do so, the fear is that the transition can be disruptive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We already have home owners with mortgages in public housing who have contractual obligations to their banks based on current valuations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What will happen if we reset prices downwards?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Even if we only roll these out for new flats, the cheaper pool of available public housing is likely to lower the resale value of the remaining existing stock.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The effects will not be limited to public housing either.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Were HDB prices to tank, private home flat prices will likely follow suit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Those who plan to extract funds to finance their retirement may suddenly find themselves with less savings than they expected and those with mortgages may find themselves underwater, where they owe the bank more than what the price of their house is worth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Banks could in turn be faced with a slew of non-performing loans and worse, if homeowners choose to forfeit their stake.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This would be a disaster scenario, not unlike the aftermath of a financial crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it does not mean that we allow a bubble to grow inexorably.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What is needed is a gentle path to this new normal so that economic growth and especially incomes can eventually catch up and make high prices justifiable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Let us start by recognising that this will not generally affect the vast majority of homeowners, either because they plan to stay put in their homes or pass it down to their children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They will face certain paper loses but this will likely be temporary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It will affect those who are currently over-invested in housing and wish to cash out for various reasons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There is already a scheme in place for this – the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) or the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS), although the details on each have yet to be ironed out in full by the Government for each case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But what do we do with those who have sold their flats?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There are, of course, the existing short-lease 2-room flexi flats, which are rationally priced according to Bala's Curve because they are always resold to HDB.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Alternatively, we can introduce limited duration public rental flats available for rent for a maximum of 10 years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, you have about a minute left.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes – since more resale flats will eventually enter the market down the road.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Hopefully, I have made it clear that there is no magic between lease and rent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For the last decade of my life, I was also a renter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I did not feel less connected to the communities where I lived nor do I feel less pride in customising the interior of my home to reflect who I was.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I saw it as a stage of my life and once I was ready for ownership, I made the transition.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We also invest in residential projects in the UK and Australia.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Previously, I was working as an urban planner with the Public Service and I studied architecture and urban studies in Singapore, the UK and the US.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: A shortage of housing and especially affordable housing is a serious problem for many cities.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Most countries and cities have some form of public, social or affordable housing programme.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Around the world, there are plenty of rousing expositions by housing authorities on their ambition to address the housing shortage and how they are going to do it.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Few actually are able to follow through and realise their plans.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: What we have achieved in Singapore is unique, special and precious.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It comes from generations of people who set enlightened policies, develop practical solutions and programmes and execute them systematically.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: When we critique our public housing programme and suggest changes, we should be careful we do not inadvertently undermine a system that works.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to discuss whether land price should be factored into the cost of public housing.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we do not have much natural resources but our 700-square kilometres of land is one of the rare natural resources we do have.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is why it makes sense to safeguard our land as a reserve.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The present Government is only a custodian and not the owner of the land.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: A piece of land has no inherent value.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Compare a piece of land in, say, Queenstown versus a similar piece of land in the middle of a huge desert.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Unless there is oil underneath, the land in the desert is not worth much.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: So, why is this piece of land in Queenstown worth so much more?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We have a vibrant economy, functioning tripartism, harmonious society, many talented and hardworking people and Singapore is one of the most liveable cities in Asia.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The public, private and people sectors work hard to make Singapore successful.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: There are also direct investments made from taxpayers' money to make the land useful and more valuable.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the investment put into building an operating Changi Airport and the various maritime ports connects us to international travel and trade routes.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: There are also investments into laying the roads, MRT lines, sewers, water pipelines, power supply, optic fibre, tree planting and recreational parks.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: When our investment creates value, we need to be able to capture it and channel back to the state or our reserves so they can be reinvested to create more value.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not factor the value of land into the cost of public housing, we are creating an open loop for the land value to be given away for free.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Some part of the society will enjoy a significant windfall from the free land while another part of society will be paying for the windfall.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It also prevents undue windfall for certain people only.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I would like to talk about public housing prices in mature estates.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Calling an HDB estate mature has come to mean better location and more desirability.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Many have implied that their higher prices are somehow the failure of HDB or the Government.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: When we buy a product that is of better quality, has more special features or it is a well-recognised status symbol, we do not question why it is more expensive.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is because we know we are paying for the additional utilitarian and experiential value.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Someone explained to me that this logic does not apply to HDB flats because public housing is a public good.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Because it is a necessity, prices should not differ too much between mature and non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To consider public housing as a public good catering to those who are needy is perhaps true in many other countries or cities.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Because they are unable to scale up their public or affordable housing programme, they are only able to cater to a small proportion of the population, perhaps 20% or significantly less.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We can academically assume that up to the 80th percentile income earners live in public housing, although I suspect many Singaporeans who belong to even higher income brackets also live in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we cannot look at people living in public housing in Singapore as a homogenous group.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We have low-income earners, middle-income earners and a good proportion of rather affluent Singaporeans living in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Mature estates command higher prices because they tend to be closer to town, have more established amenities, been renewed and upgraded.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Their prices are higher because they offer more of what people desire.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Their prices are higher because people are prepared to pay more to live there.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If we artificially suppress their prices through some form of price controls, additional subsidies or grants to buyers, we will be distorting the real prices.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Mature estates will be severely over-subscribed, which will lead to some form of balloting in order to allocate.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The winners of the ballots would enjoy disproportionate benefit compared to those who did not.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's public housing programme has gone way beyond providing just for necessity.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It has been providing for wants and aspirations for some time now.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Needs can be better defined but wants are much more difficult.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Housing needs can refer to shelter function, basic amenities and transportation access.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Housing wants can refer to location, views, size, lifestyle, special amenities, such as being near certain branded schools.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we are not facing a severe housing shortage.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Non-mature estates are well-planned, well-built, well-served by necessary amenities and public transport.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, is living in the mature estate a necessity or a non-essential?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To what extent should we use taxpayers' money or our reserves to fulfil non-essential demands of a specific group of people?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the Government's responsibility should not be extended indefinitely and it has to stop somewhere.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not forget the so-called mature estates were once new towns.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: So, buying into a non-mature estate and paying lower prices can be a good option because they will be tomorrow's mature estates.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I would now like to talk about the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) programme.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us think of SERS as a means to intensify land use.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Many older HDB estates are built to lower densities and specifications.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In land-scarce Singapore, SERS help to optimise the use of land.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: SERS also has another very important function, that is, urban renewal.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Many cities around the world face the problem of urban degeneration in their older city core or ageing estates.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Buildings, infrastructure and local community degenerates through time if they are not regularly renewed.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Older buildings are built to lower specifications and are less able to meet new expectations.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, many older HDB flats are not designed for universal access.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Without urban renewal, estates go from degeneration into decay.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: People will move out and property values will fall drastically.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For many city authorities, they are unable to effectively carry out urban renewal because it is very costly.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It is challenging to acquire existing properties or relocate people living there.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, many city authorities put substantial resources into developing new districts on unencumbered land while leaving older neighbourhoods to fend for themselves.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: When a precinct goes through SERS, there is an uplifting effect on the surrounding neighbourhood as well.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: New amenities are introduced, more young people move in, some infrastructure also get upgraded, the vitality and attractiveness of the surrounding older neighbourhoods are also improved as a result.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Urban renewal is not a one-time affair but a continuous effort.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Each SERS project requires a lot of capital.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To have a sustainable renewal programme, there has to be a sustainable way to fund it.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, as so much public funds are involved, a strict discipline must be maintained in its execution.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The methodology of valuing and pricing old as well as new flats in a SERS programme must follow a consistent and established professional practice and public policy.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This allows the Government to properly assess the feasibility of each SERS project and carry it out according to plans.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This will open the doorway for manipulation and other dire consequences.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Valuation and pricing must be rational and untainted by emotions.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is not to say we ignore the plight of the individuals who may have extenuating circumstances.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Assistance can be offered through separate designed schemes based on a different set of policies.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to talk about trade-offs in public policy making.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Public policies and programmes have a multitude of imperatives to fulfil.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: These different imperatives converge and contradict at the same time.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They also have to cater to a multitude of stakeholders with very different needs and wants.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: An enlightened public leader will carefully weigh the pros and cons of each policy option, never downplay the trade-offs and never sacrifice the long-term benefits for short-term gratification.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The enlightened leader will choose the most optimal pathway that best meets the policy objective.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Whichever path is taken, some will be more adversely affected than others.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This does not mean the policy has failed.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As I said earlier, a separate support measure can be introduced for those who are seriously affected.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We should upkeep such an enlightened way of discussing and making public policies.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They ended up making very poor choices for themselves.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Eventually, it is still the people and the man-in-the-street that suffered the most.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: What worries me is our sense of Singapore's vulnerability seems to be eroding.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is perhaps because we have been doing so well for such a long time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: HDB will continue to monitor housing demand and make adjustments, where necessary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These statements were first made known in December 2021, after a broad suite of property cooling measures were introduced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We had another round of cooling measures in September 2022, with a particular focus on the HDB market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, following multiple Parliamentary Questions (PQs) and speeches by myself and other fellow Members of Parliament, iterations of statements quoting the "up to 100,000 flats" from 2021 to 2025 figure remain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I say that there is a clear need today for not just 100,000 flats in total from 2021 to 2025 but certainly more, and it is clearly necessary to make adjustments urgently.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The objective of my speech today is thus a very simple one: for the Government to urgently execute on the policy to boost the supply of housing to address the shortfall in the market today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is not difficult to see manifestations of the severe demand-supply imbalance in our housing market today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the latest fourth quarter 2022 housing data release, HDB resale prices continue to remain firm, rising 2.3% from the last quarter, with the increase higher than the 2.1% quarter-on-quarter increase initially estimated for the quarter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was in spite of the cooling measures introduced in September 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Private residential prices, similarly, rose in spite of rising interest rates, though the extent of increase is ironically nowhere near that of the public housing market, with 2022 price increases of 8.6%, while in the last three years, prices were up by 22.8%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To put it simply, resale HDB prices are rising far more rapidly compared to private residential prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, there appears to be some signs of moderation in the private residential market, with prices up just 0.4% quarter-on-quarter versus 3.8% a quarter ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The residential rental market is, for lack of a better word, in an even scarier situation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Private residential rents rose by 7.4% in the most recent quarter alone, with rents up 30% in one year and 42% over the last three years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While HDB does not publish a rental index, a comparison of median rentals across HDB towns paints a similar uncomfortable picture.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And just a few days ago, Shin Min Daily News reported that a 74-year-old HDB unit at Seng Poh Road was rented out at $6,200 a month.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For 4-room HDB flats, median rents have risen by 22% to 50% in the last one year alone, with median rents up 29% to 68% in the last three years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And these are just a comparison of median rents, and to paraphrase what one of my residents at an earlier Meet-the-People Session (MPS) shared with me when I quoted median rents in the market, he asked me to try and go on PropertyGuru to see whether you can find such low rents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is not hard to imagine how the rental market got so out-of-hand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Private residential vacancy rates are hovering near historical lows, at 5.5% as of the fourth quarter of 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For the HDB market, in response to my Parliamentary Question in October last year, MND shared that over the past five years, the annual average number of unoccupied HDB units ranged from about 1,400 to 3,900.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These units make up a mere 0.1% to 0.4% of completed flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While multiple rounds of cooling measures in the past have typically focused on the demand side of the home purchasing equation, fundamentally, I believe the shortage in supply is a key contributing factor causing the imbalances we see in the market today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that compared to 2021, housing supply is set to increase by about 35% over 2022 and 2023, with about 23,000 BTO flats to be launched per year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the HDB stated that it is prepared to launch up to 100,000 flats in total from 2021 to 2025, if needed, subject to prevailing demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These numbers, however, need to be put in context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, while the average of 20,000 BTO flats between 2021 and 2025 is an increase compared to an average of 17,000 flats between 2016 and 2020, this is still 13% below the average of 23,000 flats in 2011 to 2015, during the time when Mr Khaw Boon Wan was Minister for National Development and sought to address the backlog in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have already seen BTO application rates climb steadily over the past decade to new highs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For 3-room and larger flats, this increased from 2.8 times in 2012 to 6.1 times in 2021 and 5.5 times in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Including 2-room flexi flats and on an overall basis, BTO application rates have climbed from about 2.8 times in 2012 to 5.6 times in 2021 and 5.1 times in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is of greater concern is that despite the ramp-up in supply with 35% more units last year, overall application rates have remained stubbornly high at 5.1 times in 2022, compared to an average of just over three times in the past decade – suggesting that the level of demand-supply imbalance remains a critical concern.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The issue of supply shortages is not unique to just the public residential sector but, similarly, applies to the private residential market as well, given the similar approach taken by the Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must, however, put these numbers into context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last year saw the lowest annual primary sales volumes across private housing and EC units in the last 14 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But there were about 8,600 units being sold.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More than 36% of the number of units made available in new supply in 2022, if we consider the last 10-year average primary sales volumes of about 12,000 units, then essentially, last year's supply is just about half of the average annual sales volume.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is no wonder that the level of unsold inventory in the private residential market is hovering near historical low levels today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And as I have shared earlier, private residential vacancy rates are hovering near historical lows.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, it is not as if we are looking at "ghost towns" being built.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If, and even if, there truly are excesses, whether in the short run or medium run, these can be repurposed into public rental flats which my hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has elaborated on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fortunately, or unfortunately, the private sector has its way of adding to residential supply through en bloc and redevelopment schemes, which partially mitigates the supply situation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A cursory look at the new launches for 2023 would suggest that a significant number of them are derived not from GLS, but also from en bloc and redevelopments concluded over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What, then, has been the key drivers of residential demand?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In response to my Parliamentary Question in October, MND shared that demand for housing has been broad-based.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On this point, I fully agree with the Government's assessment of demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More households are forming as the echo-boomer generation are getting married, especially with the easing of COVID-19 measures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We also see societal trends shifting to smaller households, as young couples, singles, as well as adult children, choose to buy their own homes instead of living with their parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, I have observed that the growth in resident households has, over the past decade, consistently outpaced that of the resident population.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, there could be a minority of citizens who can purchase private residential housing as their first home, but even ignoring demand from other groups of Singaporeans, the number of flats appears to be insufficient to meet even the demands of our newly-weds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The shrinking of overall average household sizes also does not appear to be letting up, at 3.15 as of 2021, the lowest recorded figure since 1990 when it was over 4.2.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: MND, too, noted in a Parliamentary Question response in November 2022, that over the past 20 years, the average household size among resident households living in HDB flats shrank from 3.57 to 3.09.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For the near future, MND expects housing demand to be robust due to strong household formation and societal trends towards smaller households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My question, then, is if it is already a known fact to the Government that the demand for housing is broad-based and it is unlikely that societal trends are going to go into reverse anytime soon, should we not take more proactive steps to address demand from Singaporeans, rather than try to curb demand?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, I believe net immigration into Singapore could add further strain on local housing demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the latest labour market report for the third quarter of 2022, MOM noted that the labour market maintained its growth momentum in the quarter, as total employment continued to expand robustly, led by non-residents at 71,100, compared to residents at 4,800.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are seeing high occupancy rates at dormitories as the number of Work Permit holders in the Construction, Marine and Process (CMP) sectors is currently at more than 10% higher than pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Two weeks ago, The Straits Times reported that record-high HDB rents and difficulties in securing accommodation are driving Malaysians working in Singapore to live in Johor Bahru and commute to Singapore daily for work instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should the non-resident labour force continue to grow, this could continue to add further strain on our already strained housing market situation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In October last year, I asked if additional sites can be activated to increase the number of HDB BTO flat launches beyond the current plan to launch up to 100,000 flats in total, from 2021 to 2025, should demand exceed current projections and if not, what are the constraints for not being able to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Apart from reiterating existing plans to launch up to 100,000 flats between 2021 and 2025, I do not think I got a response to my question.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, if we look at the HDB BTO launches over the last 10 years, approximately half of the sites used for public housing developments over the past 10 years were greenfield.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In comparison to brownfield sites, and certainly so for sites which are already located within existing housing estates, there need not be as much land preparation works that need to be done.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just last month, the hon Mr Gan Thiam Poh even asked whether the open land between TPE and Fernvale Street will be used to build HDB BTO flats to meet the increased demand for public housing and if so, when will HDB flats be built there.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note that based on the URA's gazetted Master Plan 2019, plot ratios for certain sites have even been determined at 2.1 and 3.5, with the road name Fernvale Crescent also decided.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, like Mr Gan, I too hope MND will launch HDB flats at Fernvale Crescent soon.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am comforted by Prime Minister Lee's comments during the National Day Rally late last year, where he shared that and I quote, "We have done our studies and planning.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We will have enough space for future generations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our problem is not finding the space to build enough flats, nor keeping homes affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We know how to do that." I, thus, sincerely hope the Government can take urgent and decisive steps to increase the availability of public housing and ensure that the housing needs of all Singaporeans are met.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to conclude in Mandarin, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government often stresses that home ownership has been, and will always be Singapore's key housing strategy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These numbers, however, need to be put in context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, while the average of 20,000 BTO flats between 2021 to 2025 is an increase compared to average of 17,000 flats between 2016 and 2020, this is still 13% below the average of 23,000 flats in 2011 to 2015, during the time when Mr Khaw Boon Wan was Minister for National Development and sought to address the backlog in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have already seen BTO application rates climbing steadily over the past decade to new highs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last September, I tabled an Adjournment Motion in Parliament to call on the Government to take decisive steps to increase the availability of public housing and solve the imbalance between supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said during the National Day Rally 2022 that “our problem is not finding the space to build enough flats, nor keeping homes affordable for Singaporeans”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, I sincerely hope the Government can seriously consider our request and the people's request by ensuring an adequate supply of public housing to help Singaporeans realise their home ownership dream.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The original public housing policy intent: the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, founding Prime Minister of Singapore, has placed public housing as a key pillar of the People's Action Party (PAP) mandate to improve the living standards for its people.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Ensuring that citizens have a roof over their heads, and later, promoting home ownership, is the paramount priority of the PAP Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, as Singapore progresses, HDB flats also evolved to meet the changing needs and expectations of residents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We see the building of beautiful housing landmarks, such as The Pinnacle@Duxton and Punggol 21.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of them are comparable to, and even look better than private leasehold developments, and at less than half the prices.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our CPF relaxation also means that many times, there is no cash outlay and one can tap on CPF to pay one's mortgage.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Such is the success and appeal of Singapore's national housing programme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But is Singapore a victim of its own successful public housing policy, some asked.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Singaporeans now see owning an HDB flat as a rite of passage and even an entitlement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The initial goal of HDB to provide a home for every Singaporean has long been surpassed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In an effort to accommodate the changing needs and aspirations of residents, HDB has now given owners the flexibility to both own HDB and private properties, and even renting out their HDB flats while living in private properties.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is, thus, not a surprise that a number of Singaporeans see an HDB flat as an investment vehicle to make a windfall profit upon sale.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some purchase private properties after their Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) and rent out their HDB flats as a source of passive rental income.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have even heard of instances when HDB homes were sold in the market immediately after MOP and advertised to be "hardly lived in" or "as good as new".
