speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The popularity of mature estates: Sir, I believe that the popularity of mature estates is the elephant in the room.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The returns appear to be even higher for those who are lucky enough to procure an HDB flat in or closer to the city or mature estates, the more popular places.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The popularity of mature estates has led to excessive demand, longer wait times and a reluctance to consider other locations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It has also led to some uniquely Singaporean behaviours of courting couples in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst applying for an HDB flat used to mean a serious intent to settle down for marriage, it is not always so now.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know of couples who apply for an HDB flat within a few months of courtship, citing the long waiting times for a matrimonial home.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is helpful to those, especially my residents in the Central District, who want to buy with the interest to stay, especially in the prime locations and mature estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Alas, it may be too late for HDB to turn back the clock entirely and revert to the policy of only insisting that one must live in one's HDB flat, disallow one to purchase a private property whilst owning an HDB flat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Needs and aspirations of home owners have changed over time and some flexibility is to be expected.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the fundamental purpose and priority of public housing has to remain to provide for affordable housing for each Singaporean household to live in.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The key, now, Sir, is then to balance between home owner-occupation and investment, and second, to manage the demand for HDB flats in popular mature estates versus non-mature estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on balancing between home owner-occupation and investment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, continue to apply the principles of the PLH scheme to the popular and mature HDB estates, to further strengthen the owner-occupation intent of public housing and to weaken the investment intent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Where need be, the Government must have the moral courage to apply the same principles to all HDB estates with stricter applications to the popular locales.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Industries, professionals and potential buyers I spoke to have found that this ABSD measure is effective.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My suggestion is to make a bigger distinction between the ABSD that Singaporeans have to pay versus Permanent Residents (PRs) and foreigners, to ensure that Singapore properties will be less costly to Singaporeans and will remain mostly in Singaporeans' hands.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If non-Singaporeans wish to purchase more Singapore properties, they should pay a higher price.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on balancing the appeal of mature versus non-mature estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to engineer demand away from popular mature estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Like what Nominated Member of Parliament Cheng Hsing Yao mentioned, is it "a must-have" or "a nice-to-have", to stay in a popular estate?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: HDB should engineer a change to shift demand away from the mature estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: HDB has done it before and can do it again.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Bishan, once unpopular because it was a former graveyard is now one of the most sought-after, due to good schools and excellent public transport connections.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The new town of Punggol with its waterway, parks and jetty, and a proposed Punggol District Park is another.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not uncommon to hear of governments in other countries providing very attractive incentives to entice people, citizens to relocate to targeted residential zones.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, do more for couples embarking on marriage and parenthood, especially first-timer applicants.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Take a calculated risk at least in the short term to Build-Then-Order, to advance build for this group, building in advance, instead of just Build-To-Order.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am really glad that the Minister is considering shorter waiting time flats and I would urge him to consider an even shorter or no waiting time flat for these genuine first-timers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope I have heard the proposal correctly because Mr Leong has moved from his former position of excluding land cost totally from BTO flats to now, a deferred land cost.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: According to this proposal, from what I heard, a buyer will need to pay only: one, a construction cost; and two, a notional location cost, when he buys a flat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I guess it will just take one to two years of one's annual pay to pay up this flat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And, if the owner decides to stay, then he will get to keep the flat at $140,000.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Leong is indeed proposing a very big Valentine's Day gift of a double subsidy to every Singaporean BTO buyer.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wonder how this will be financed or traded-off against other national needs, such as healthcare, education, not to mention the current housing deficits.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How does Mr Leong's proposal address the elephant in the room that I have mentioned, that mature estates in prime locations are still highly sought after?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How does Mr Leong's proposal address this elephant in the room that there are still mature estates that are still very popular and how do you meet the needs of first-time owners who want to live in these prime locations?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Is this solving a housing affordability issue or just confusing the issues?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I seek Mr Leong's clarification on his proposed Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And how does the high demand for prime location, mature estate housing be addressed, versus my earlier suggestions?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is now so appealing that most young Singaporeans want to have a piece of it, want to be part of this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I do not think it is broken, but it can further evolve to ensure that priority is indeed given to fundamentally housing our citizens.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Housing policies and pricing decisions everywhere in the world are complex and involve decisions that affect economic, social and political stability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot just reboot or reset at will.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I urge Singaporeans not to be taken in by populist suggestions to undermine our precious national public housing programme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I support the Motion by the Minister for National Development.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And that is why you cannot transfer land at historical cost, at $1 or whatever.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because you must make the HDB management and the board accountable for all its operations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: When you do it at less than market price, they are going to have a field day with what they want to do.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The second point that was raised was whether this amounted to a raid on our reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To be very, very honest, my brain is not very big and it is not very fast.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It took me a while to figure out why Minister Desmond Lee said it amounted to a raid on reserves – and it is.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I have not discussed this with Minister Desmond Lee, but I hope I get it correct.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Let us say there is a piece of land here.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The authority – whether it is the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) or the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) – can decide to give this piece of land to HDB to develop.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But on the other hand, it can also decide to sell this same piece of land to the private sector.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai will know this because he is an Economics graduate from Japan, I think.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Are there instances where land is transferred at less than market price?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I think there are; I have not checked this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Gardens by the Bay is in a prime location.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If it is not transferred at a nominal price, it cannot be built.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Government hospitals, I think, should be transferred at nominal value because we need to build hospitals for our elderly and for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: SAF training camps and training grounds must have been transferred to the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) at a very low cost because that is for national defence.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Gardens by the Bay and public hospitals are public amenities for the public to use, for the public to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And that is why it justifies transferring the land at below market price.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But your HDB flats are public housing, but it is not a public home for the public to walk in and out.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is a home that Singaporeans own and they live in and have their own privacy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There was walk-in selection, where people walked in and they bought the walk-in flats at prices lower than those for the people who have queued for their flats.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, be careful what you wish for, because if I go by Mr Leong's methodology, we can be in a lot of trouble.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Over the Chinese New Year, I came across an article by a BBC correspondent.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is an article written in January, last month.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It says, "Japan was the future, but it is stuck in the past." Singapore was the future, is the future and, as an aspirational country, we definitely want to be the future too.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I quote, "Then in 1991, the bubble burst.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They are yet to recover." A friend was recently negotiating to buy several hectares of forest.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: My friend told him forest land is only worth $2 per square metre.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But he insisted he needed $20 a square metre because that was what he paid for in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: You go to Tokyo, you go to Osaka.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The property prices have never recovered in the last few decades.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, the song goes again – be careful what you wish for.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I wish I could sing it to you, but the Standing Orders do not allow me to sing in Chamber.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, I was reading just last night as I was trying to research for what I want to say today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: But after hearing, I decided to put aside my speech and maybe I should respond.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I think there is a quote by Lenin from Soviet Russia.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: He said something along the lines like, there are decades where nothing happens, but there are weeks where decades happen.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: If I go according to Mr Leong's or the PSP's methodology, those few weeks and those few months can see our property prices crumbling.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: What I have learnt is that when you come down it is very steep, it is very slippery, it is very fast.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: But when you try your way to recover and to climb back up, I can tell you the slope is very, very gradual.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In Hong Kong, for example, it is 51%.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, if we do what Mr Leong suggested we do, are we able to stomach it?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And another lesson I learnt in life is that when you do something, you ask yourself whether you can stomach it, because if you cannot, do not do it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Do not think about the upside because the upside is only a measurement of your happiness.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: That is something you can fully enjoy and fully be able to take in.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I think we hope to see something like a Goldilocks situation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Our prices can move steadily upwards and slowly, in line with our rise in income, not too hot, not too cold.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai gave an example about Tengah.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Actually, I was hoping that he would bring up Bidadari as an example, because Bidadari is in Potong Pasir constituency.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is more like six, of their annual income.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And I think that is fully affordable, right?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In fact, I think it is very good.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It has delivered many benefits to Singaporeans and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And that is why there are public policy adjustments from time to time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Again, I want to say, be careful what you wish for, because we are having a good run.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It has taken us 60 years, almost 60 years, to reach where we are today, because we have got hardworking people, we have got good jobs, we have got good economic growth and the nation has progressed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: But there is one more thing, one more key important reason that I feel we do not talk about enough.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And it is because the PAP Government has earned its place amongst our people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We have built upon the strength of this nation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: One people, one heart, "one semangat" or one spirit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Please allow me to first deal with the Motion in the name of the hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Mr Leong Mun Wai and to contrast it with that standing in the name of the Minister for National Development.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the first Motion, I have no quarrel with the need for this House to review public housing per se, to ensure that public housing is kept affordable, accessible and inclusive for every Singaporean of each generation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested that the second Motion precludes this review notion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not think that is the intent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong himself committed in this House that all public policies will be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But he also said that the values that the PAP Government stands for, that remains firm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And the values embedded in this Motion, about providing our Singaporeans with affordable and accessible housing, taking care of the interest of the current and future generations of Singaporeans – those values, as far as I am concerned, are immutable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I strongly reject the insidious premise of the first Motion; that the review is required “in order” to deliver affordable and accessible housing, which is to say that this Government is not doing so now for the majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Respectfully, there is no basis for this allegation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will show why this first Motion rings hollow and sounds naive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This makes Singapore as having the highest rate of homeownership in the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In comparison, close to 70% of European Union residents own their homes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Switzerland, it is about 39%, in the UK and US, it is about 65%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The United Nations (UN)-Habitat issues publications to provide reliable and independent documentation of housing programmes across the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, the quality of public housing in Singapore is high.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Nominated Member of Parliament Mr Cheng Hsing Yao spoke eloquently about this and the factors that have contributed to this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is embedded with various upgrading programmes, at a cost that is borne largely by public funds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is supportive infrastructure and amenities too like MRT stations, schools, shopping centres, swimming pools, sporting stadia and other facilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need only ask the well-travelled Singaporeans amongst us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fair-minded will say that we compare very favourably and I fully agree with the hon Nominated Member of Parliament Mr Cheng that Singapore is one of the most liveable countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The UN-Habitat report is from a reputable international organisation that does not have to humour Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What the hon Non-Constituency Members of Parliament have suggested in their Motion is at variance with the report.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now let me outline the difference between the first Motion and the second Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first states aspirations without cost – hence, it is naive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first speaks as if everyone is entitled; the second requires us to respect the differences in society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, it requires that the Government balances the different interests within the current generation, showing us that there are contestations among different groups even today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this, the Government's philosophy has been socialist – that the least among us must have the most.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, the Motion requires us to make a difficult political choice – to be fair, not just to the citizens of today, but to those of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is difficult because we must resist the political temptation to pander to the voters of today who decide based on the tangible benefits which they can see and experience, rather than any notions of fairness to people to whom they owe nothing – the citizens of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And yet, this PAP Government is a strange creature that feels this debt and in housing, as in so many other policies, including most recently, climate change adaptation, it has committed itself to the long-term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On housing affordability, it may be useful to bear in mind how Singapore compares with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the middle-income households, this translates to 31%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, they spend most of their money on housing as compared to other essentials such as food and clothing, education and health.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) Members of Parliament dispute this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They feel that the servicing of the mortgages through the CPF presents a cost, even though it may not be accompanied by cash payment for most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, I want to highlight that you can only use the Ordinary Account of the CPF to fund housing instalments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Special Account is preserved, the Retirement Account is preserved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the end of the day, what is the PSP referring to as cost?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, when the people, the residents pay through CPF and when they sell their house, they get a refund, it is really to secure their retirement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, if this is not a good idea, then what is PSP's proposal to take care of the retirement needs of such people?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, in the 2022 Urban Land Institute Asia Pacific Home Attainability Index, Singapore’s public housing was ranked as the most affordable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do recognise that there are fellow Singaporeans who feel that housing has become very expensive and out of their reach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, one third of the cases in my Meet-the People Sessions now relate to housing matters – and quite a few of them are young people who are in the queue for flats, just like what Mr Sitoh Yih Pin had said.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, I want to acknowledge that they are anxious because the wait has been longer than expected for their flats and with rents being so expensive, the pain of the wait is very real.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is difficult, but useful, for us to distinguish the problem of a delay in getting a flat with the problem of affordability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The comparison I gave just now, as well as the fact that many Singaporeans can service their mortgages through CPF alone speaks volumes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the problem of delay, as may be recalled, buildings across the world was affected by the pandemic and Singapore is no exception.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Ms Hazel Poa has suggested ramping it up to the numbers we saw in the 1980s, but is that a wise idea?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I cannot put it better than what Mr Sitoh had said.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Be careful of what you wish for, because if you were to do it wrongly, then the sellers will get upset.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then we will get back to Parliament and somebody will be making arguments on behalf of the sellers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, it has to be a very calibrated approach to make sure that you build in accordance with what the market can absorb, at the same time, deal with the aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Hong Kong, it was announced that they are building 30,000 temporary public housing units over a five-year period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a temporary solution and it seems to me that they have a more difficult housing problem.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current waiting time in Hong Kong was reported to be 5.6 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With this temporary solution, the government intends to cut it down to 4.5 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Ms Poa had suggested the waiting time should also include time of an unsuccessful applicant, but as what the hon Minister had said, there are many, many ways for one to acquire, or several ways for one to acquire a BTO flat.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: You can apply for an SBF flat, you can apply for a BTO flat in a mature estate and you can apply for a BTO flat in a non-mature estate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To just blanketly measure waiting time for all these cases together does not make sense, but qualitatively, we are already measuring it, because for those in a non-mature estate, they get priority and the Minister already said they will get their flat within three tries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore ownership figures I highlighted does not, however, speak for the 3% in our population of Singapore residents who cannot afford to own their homes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For them, they are provided with public rental housing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This compares favourably with a number of other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Hong Kong, it is 29% for social housing units; for Netherlands, it is 32%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Monthly rents payable by Singaporeans depend on their household income.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Although global comparisons are available, it makes the most sense to compare such rents against the next available option in Singapore – the private market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members will not be surprised to hear that such rooms go for 10 to 20 times more in the private market, even on a shared basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, I should also mention that our Government has specific policies to support households in rental flats to own homes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I hope I have shown the underlying socialist bent in our public housing policy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: During the chaos of the 1960s, many Singaporeans lived in squalor and only 9% of our population was in public housing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew envisioned a Singapore where all Singaporeans will own their own flats so that they will have tangible stakes in our nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Housing can drive progress in connected areas such as better education outcomes from our children who live in better conditions, higher productivity and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With economic growth and generations of surpluses, we can then invest more in public housing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That was the virtuous circle that Mr Lee and his team built.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That may have sounded like a pipedream then.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But, almost 60 years later, it is clear we have made substantial progress in achieving this vision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore has been transformed and Singaporeans' fortunes have changed for the better.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai said that historically, units were sold without HDB accounting for land cost.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I dispute that, because when I looked at the financial statements of HDB, they have calculated that since 1960, about $40-plus billion was owed by HDB in relation to the land cost of the land upon which public housing was provided.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is monitored and it is certainly in the books.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our Government continues to invest heavily in public housing programmes, building affordable and high-quality public housing estates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the investments and policies are carefully calibrated to ensure that the interests of future generations of Singaporeans are protected too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Much credit for this belongs to the past and present officers of HDB who were encouraged to think boldly and creatively to deliver on its mission of providing affordable and high-quality public housing units to generations of Singaporeans who have ever higher expectations and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We owe them a huge debt of thanks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These officers and those in the Ministry of Finance (MOF) too, think of Singapore as an immortal being playing an infinite game.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This means planning for the very long term and, as an economist said, "We will all be dead but our children and grandchildren and everyone we care for still live on." With respect, having regard to what has happened over the past six decades, for the hon Non-Constituency Members of Parliament to insinuate through this Motion that public housing in Singapore is neither affordable nor accessible is rather rich.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may be an opportune time for me to deal with the point that hon Member Leong Mun Wai made in his speech in this House about the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said VERS is not a viable solution to the lease decay problem.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was because Singaporeans are expecting VERS to be like the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) for all, meaning there is an expectation for residents to be paid.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, I question the hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament's assumption that Singaporeans are expecting VERS to be like SERS for all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may be useful to understand the factual context clearly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A person buying a BTO flat, say, in his early 30s, will get a 99-year lease.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such a case, there will be a more than sufficient remainder of the lease at the point of his retirement in his 60s or 70s.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This asset can be monetised through programmes such as the Silver Housing Bonus scheme or Lease Buyback Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these can provide them with decent financial support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Leong Mun Wai appears to be averse to such monetisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How then would you support some people in these situations who want to enhance their retirement expenditure?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For those who have purchased resale flats, they would know the remaining length of the leaseholds beforehand.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would allow them to make informed choices before purchasing the resale flats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, they may decide to purchase resale flats that may have substantial remainders that will allow them to monetise the assets like owners of BTO flats or they can decide to buy leaseholds which are long enough for them to stay in their homes until the end of their lives, which will naturally mean that the opportunity to monetise their assets will not be as good.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whatever the reasons, they know when the leaseholds apart will expire.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Against this context, it seems to me unreasonable for a person who purchase a resale flat, knowing full well when the leasehold expires, to then expect to get compensation that is substantially more than the value of the tail end of the leasehold under VERS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may be useful to remember what the Prime Minister said in his 2018 National Day Rally speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He specifically made the point that there was not much financial upside to VERS as compared to SERS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given what the Prime Minister had said, I struggle to understand why the hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Leong Mun Wai contends that Singaporeans are expecting VERS to be like SERS for all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What he is in fact asking Singaporeans is to dream an impossible dream and then ask the Government to make it true.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we were kind, we would say he is being naive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But if we were honest, we would say something else.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek Mr Leong Mun Wai's permission to engage in a thought experiment to better understand the proposal that PSP made in its manifesto for General Elections 2020 – compulsory SERS for all old flats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That was the alternative to the PAP's VERS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we were to go back to what the Prime Minister has suggested or rather dealt with in his 2018 speech, he referred to three estates – Bedok, Ang Mo Kio and Marine Parade.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He mentioned that all of them were built around the same time, between the 1970s and the early-1980s.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They probably have about at least 117,000 units.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If all these flats were to be SERS-ed, what would be the compensation that PSP proposes to pay, given the position that Mr Leong Mun Wai took in his Adjournment Motion?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He would very well know the compensation that Ang Mo Kio SERS units get.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I understand, that is the market rate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is being suggested is a higher rate so that there is some cash from VERS – just like SERS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for Mr Leong Mun Wai's elucidation of the PSP's proposal that there should be compulsory SERS for all flats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the Motion standing in the name of the Minister for National Development.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the Motion for its underlying philosophy of socialism and its long-term policy orientation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, as I alluded to earlier, the importance of ensuring that our public housing scheme provides all Singaporeans with access to affordable homes extends to well beyond the specific purpose of providing roofs over our heads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One area that I am concerned about is how our housing policy is connected with the development of human capital.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore has done quite well in this area.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Murali, you have slightly over a minute left.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I will just make this suggestion and I will go to my conclusion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This presents a problem for HDB because as a matter of policy, it does not directly allocate homes to persons to be fair to all Singaporeans in the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, what I am suggesting, Sir, is for a system to be implemented, which allows HDB to provide inputs upstream during the divorce proceedings so that this can be taken into consideration by the Court to make a just and equitable decision with regard to the needs of the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I chose the second Motion over the first not because of any partisan politics but because I prefer the hard truths over soft lies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There is no point in making vainglorious promises without a way to deliver.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There is no courage in forsaking the future for the present.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These are the two fatal flaws of the first Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The second Motion commits us to providing affordable housing to Singaporeans today in a way that bends the laws of the market to give the most to those who have the least.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It also commits us to an ideal beyond the political – that all of us in this House owe a duty as much to the Singaporeans of tomorrow as those of today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The second Motion asks a lot of us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is by no means an easier choice but I believe it is the right one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick clarification for the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai on a point he made about legacy land costs in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I just confirm which annual report is he referring to?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because at page 50 of the latest annual report, there is a reference to accumulated Government grants provided to HDB since its establishment in 1960 and that is $42 billion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But that does not refer to land costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just want to understand from Mr Murali Pillai – is that the figure he is referring to?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because my understanding is, it is not referring to land costs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That was indeed what I was referring to.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It was in relation to what the HDB had paid or committed to pay to the Government for the land that was used to build the HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just to confirm the statement in the annual report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It refers to the annual deficit in HDB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: HDB's annual deficit is fully covered by a Government grant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In addition, HDB receives a Government grant to preserve the capital gains attributable to past governments on disposal of the protected assets in accordance with the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I am not sure whether the land cost is specifically $40 billion, as stated by the Member.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I took it as the grants being the equivalent to the land cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my speech, I mentioned the building rates in the 1980s.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not suggesting that we build the same number of flats as we did in the 1980s.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I did is to use that as an illustration of what is possible, not that we should build exactly the same number.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, this is not an opportunity for another speech, just for quick clarifications.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am responding to what other Members have said.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Just now, Miss Cheryl Chan also made the point that if we increased the supply of flats, how that will impact the resale prices and whether people will still be able to sell their resale flats to fund their retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can I clarify in effect what she is saying is that we are controlling the supply of new flats in order to keep up the prices in the resale market?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Because the fact is that when you have a shrinking population, we may or may not even have buyers for these future owners of such BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The residents appealing are likely couples about to get married or couples already married and looking to start a family or, indeed, couples with a child.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: By the time they move into a BTO flat four to five years later, they would be in their mid- or late-30s.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, resale is not an option because prices have shot up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, their appeal is either to please help them get a good number in the upcoming BTO exercise because they simply cannot afford to lose more time in trying again in a subsequent exercise or, more starkly, the second type of appeal, please help them get a Sale of Balance Flat (SBF) because they need a unit available immediately.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have also had parents reaching out to me on behalf of their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, it is not only young couples who are concerned, but also their parents who have themselves gone through their housing journey with the nation, raised their children in HDB homes and are now watching to see if their children will also benefit from our housing policies the same way that they have.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Top of mind for these Singaporeans, I think, is housing accessibility – as in whether I can get a flat and get it fast, in time for my life plans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Then, there is the issue of affordability – whether I can pay for the flat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Accessibility and affordability – two operative words in the Motions before this House.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They feed into each other and I will speak on both.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But let me speak first on accessibility as it is more top of mind for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And there does not seem to be enough of these.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And then, there are Singaporeans who are getting BTOs, but rueing the four- to five-year wait time to collect keys.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Taken together, they point to a general conclusion, that perhaps, we should have many more BTO units with much shorter wait times in our system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be fair, the Government had already rolled out BTO flats with shorter wait times before COVID-19 and even after COVID-19 made construction delays the dominant issue, never mind building ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: By the BTO exercise in November 2021, HDB was able to resume the launch of flats with shorter wait times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, a sharp ramp-up in BTO units with Shorter Wait Times, and I would add, quite a remarkable ramp-up too, a decisive ramp-up, straight out of the gates of COVID-19 disruption.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I would note too, that a number of these projects drew first-timer application rates of only 1.5, 1.9, two times, for 4- and 5-room units – quite low, despite the wait times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, the market is telling us something about the latent demand for shorter wait times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, I strongly believe that we can and should do more, in terms of providing many more flats with much shorter wait times, partly because our experience today is pointing to a real need for this solution, and partly because I believe that this is a case where demand for shorter wait times can be induced by the right amount of supply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Flats with shorter wait times should become an anchor product, a staple, in our future BTO launch inventory.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They should make up a larger portion of our annual supply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This would certainly be useful for first-timer couples who are marrying later in life, or those who are 	already married but looking to settle in their own "nest" before starting a family and certainly for those already with a child.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Building more flats ahead of demand would increase the risk of over-supply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, this risk, I think, is well manageable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, my suggestion will not solve the current supply crunch because it will take three or more years for the higher supply of shorter wait times to enter the market.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, this is a suggestion for the longer term, given our experience today, in order to reduce the likelihood and the effects of a repeat experience in future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For the current supply crunch, we simply have to launch more, which the Government is already doing, and to build fast, while maintaining standards	 and give home owners their keys as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Besides wait time, there is one more aspect to accessibility, which is the success rate at BTO exercises.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Success rate – getting a number to choose a flat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On this, there are anecdotal accounts of difficulties with the ballot, but let us look at the overall system objectively.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The average first-timer application rate across these units was 1.85, under two.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, very good chances really for first-timers to secure one of these 4- or 5-room BTO units.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, these units drew only 28% of all first-timer applications for 4- or 5-room units.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Where did the rest of the applications go?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Let us look at the most popular flat types in 2022 – 4-room in Geylang, first-timer application rate of 20.5%; 5-room in Tampines, in August, 18.5%; and 4-room in Tampines, the same project, 17.2%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Together, these account for only 3% of 4- and 5-room BTO units launched, but they attracted 16% of all first-timer applications for the whole of 2022.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, 3% of units drawing 16% of applications on one hand versus 60% of units, drawing only 28% of applications.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, the perception of low chances in BTO exercises is really driven by the concentration of applications in a small number of projects.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Whereas for the many other projects available, applicants do stand good chances, on average.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, as the Minister  and HDB have said, virtually, all first-timer families who apply for BTO flats in non-mature estates succeed within three tries.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, on the count of balloting for BTO flats, our overall system is, in fact, doing well, producing outcomes and we should give recognition when it is due.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the Motion standing in the names of Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa clearly states that "This House calls upon the Government to review its public housing policies in order to deliver affordable and accessible HDB flats to all Singaporeans" – affordable and accessible flats to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I heard Mr Leong Mun Wai's suggestion about the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Basically, deferring of a major cost component, vastly cheaper flats.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And going by the language in his Motion, I assume that he means for these affordable homes to be accessible to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: What does he think will happen to the resale market?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And does he not agree that he seriously risks crashing the resale market instead of keeping it buoyant, as he has claimed?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can he expect to keep the resale market buoyant with such a shock?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, for those first-timers who, for whatever reason, have to buy a resale flat, they will have to pay full market value by his proposal because the seller has to pay back the deferred price component to HDB.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, what happens to equitable access for all first-timers?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can Mr Leong Mun Wai shed some light on this?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To the Workers’ Party, I think in their Facebook post, they had highlighted anxieties over one's chances in BTO applications, especially for mature estates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But what would be the Workers' Party's position on addressing this issue of one's chances for a mature estate BTO?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because the reality is that there is no easy solution.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, would the Workers' Party be prepared or be minded to acknowledge this reality to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Over the last two years, the Workers' Party has put forth in this House the proposition that Singaporeans' housing needs are becoming more diverse and hence, we should have more diverse housing options.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For instance, more rental, less ownership – more options for more diverse housing needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I say that home ownership remains the dominant housing need of Singaporeans, an aspiration of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: However, I think our needs, other than housing, have become more diverse.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, our housing strategy should keep up with that.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How do we keep flats affordable, such that Singaporeans, while owning their homes, also have enough to build and live the good life in other diverse areas and fulfil increasingly diverse needs?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is the nub of the affordability issue, in my view.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: What is an affordable home in this context?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I think it starts with a cap on BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Compare these with prices under the Prime Location Public Housing (PLH) model.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the same BTO exercise, the PLH project in Kallang Whampoa has 4-room units starting at $509,000.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, the PLH model lowered prices with higher subsidies to the extent that these prices were lower than the prices at the non-PLH Ang Mo Kio Central Weave.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe we should keep any 4-room BTO flat within reach of a Singaporean family at median income.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A 4-room unit at Ang Mo Kio Central Weave, in my view, should have been capped at $500,000, and not starting from $530,000.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Similarly, I believe we should keep any 5-room BTO flat within reach of the 60th income percentile.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government’s approach has been to supply the same flat type in different locations at different price points for different budgets.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a sound approach, but what I am suggesting is to further calibrate this and to cap the upper end, based on five times current income benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This would serve as a strong psychological marker, but there is also a very important philosophical point here.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A price cap would ensure that any project, in any location, will still be within reach of a broad segment of Singaporeans and ensure that any project, in any location, will have an inclusive mix of Singaporeans living there.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the first instance, I suggest we expand the PLH model.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, one option, expand the PLH model to more projects.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I say, let us extend the PLH model into a more flexible, more finely tiered system of MOPs and subsidy recovery rates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This tiered system would allow the Government to flex the amount of additional subsidies to apply to various projects.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need that flexibility in our system of public housing subsidies, going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a bit like we now have S-size and XL-size subsidies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is time to add the M- and L-sizes in between so that, ultimately, we keep all BTO projects within reach of target segments and, at the same time, effectively mitigate the windfall effects for different projects to varying degrees.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I note that in the Workers' Party manifesto in 2020, they said, and I quote, "HDB BTO selling prices in non-mature estates should be pegged to household incomes and prices should be based on a 20-year mortgage, 10% downpayment and monthly repayments of a maximum of 25% of the median monthly household income." I did a back-of-the-envelope calculation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the Minister has already given statistics just now, showing that our non-mature estate BTO average price currently at $340,000.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, it seems like our non-mature estate BTOs are affordable by the Workers' Party's own definition of affordability.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And yet, I think in one of the Workers' Party Member's speech just now, it was premised entirely on the notion that HDB prices are high.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Are HDB prices high or are they affordable, going by what the Workers' Party themselves have said?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And to Ms Hazel Poa, she mentioned that everybody is paying for their HDB flats in some way.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I absolutely agree and the Minister himself has said so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The point is, if HDB does not pay for the land cost, according to their proposal and put back this land cost into the reserves, then what is really happening is that future generations are paying for our current generation's flats.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And as Ms Hazel Poa, herself said, "羊毛毕竟出在羊身上".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Over the past two years, many residents have shared with me their concerns about housing and buying an HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Not only young residents but also their parents have worries.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Rising resale prices and tight supply of BTOs are the personal experience of many residents.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Are the BTO flats still affordable and accessible?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: However, many first-timers still choose popular projects, adding to the crunch.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But objectively speaking, BTO flats have not become out of reach.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Of course, the accessibility of HDB flats also involves waiting time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has introduced a shorter waiting time of 2.5 to 3.8 years in November 2021.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: No system is perfect and no system should stay static.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We must continue to evolve our public housing system and evolve our social compact with Singaporeans on housing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But as it is, we have had in Singapore a heck of a public housing system and a heck of a social compact with Singaporeans on housing, that have produced a heck of a set of outcomes to date.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It started with an audacious goal to move citizens of a new nation into flats, and since then, the system has added new pillars.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Every evolution henceforth will only become more complex, to an already complex system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But we have today a great system as a strong basis for further action.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Minister Desmond Lee has said, that public housing in Singapore is social policy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A flat is a home, an anchor in our lives, a stake in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, beyond the ballot, I believe still, that a BTO home remains a promise by Singapore, to Singaporeans, a bedrock in our social compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, HDB – the Housing and Development Board – might as well also be the "Hopes and Dreams Board" – HDB.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because HDB's purpose is to build Homes, build Dreams, build a Nation, not just brick-and-mortar flats.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Have we lost our way in this regard?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The last few years, particularly with COVID-19, have presented HDB with some unprecedented challenges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the main issues faced by my residents in recent times, is not so much the affordability, but rather, the availability of BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People who want BTO flats are unable to get them and there is a long list of people applying for one, including new couples, first-timers, divorced couples looking for new homes, singles and older couples looking to downsize.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Each has their own unique needs and stories and I have appealed for many of these residents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most people I have appealed for pointed out that the big differences in prices between HDB BTOs and resale flats are the prime reason they wanted BTOs rather than going to the resale market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, I have some serious concerns with the proposal put forward by Mr Leong Mun Wai and the Progress Singapore Party (PSP).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Leong proposes pricing flats based on two components.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, construction costs and a notional premium based on location.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, at the time anyone chooses to sell, they will pay the full cost of the land.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He acknowledges the cost of the land will be the higher component, so the price they pay for land will be more than the price of the flat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Workers' Party's Mr Jamus Lim, also seems to agree with this proposal to separate the land charges from the building costs and to pass on the land charges at the time of sale.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are some important implications from the PSP's proposals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, BTO flats are not priced according to their cost.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They are instead priced based on a variety of factors linked to affordability, including ratio of income to price, mortgage serviceability and location, as the Minister had explained.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The median household, according to the Minister, would be able to afford 80% of available flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Land cost is not currently passed on to buyers, but rather it is taken into account in HDB's books when HDB uses land from our land reserves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, HDB is paying for the land cost, not the buyers of flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, the cost is currently not being passed on to the buyers directly and the current subsidy that buyers get is actually the difference between the actual cost of building the flat, which is the building cost and the land cost, against the price they actually pay.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, the way in which the flat is priced may create severe market distortions at different points in time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time they are launched, the flats will appear very cheap because they are launched only at the cost of construction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if prime area flats are not priced significantly more than other areas, then the lottery effect there would be even greater because everybody wants a prime area flat and those who get the windfall, those who succeed in getting the prime area flat will feel very happy and those who lose out will be resentful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe this would simply exacerbate the current BTO problems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Already, at current BTO prices, even non-mature estate flats are severely oversubscribed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With an initial sticker price that is even lower than the current price, the queue is probably going to explode.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I mean, who would not want a flat at that price?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those people who win the lottery to buy the flats, however, if for some reason they decide to sell their flats, they will then realise there is a huge bill to pay in terms of land costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People may need to sell their flats for any number of reasons, including changing family or financial circumstances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, it is, at that point, they will be stabbed with a huge sticker price which will be more than the price they actually paid for the flat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, even if a couple is divorcing or the family size gets smaller, say with children moving out, or bigger, or say, with children arriving or parents moving in, families will not be able to sell if they cannot stump up a large amount of cash.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ms Hazel Poa talked about the ills of Government subsidies for public housing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was a criticism of the current scheme where HDB provides a house below the price of building it and has to make up for this deficit from the current Budget every year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: She is correct that all of us, all Singaporeans are subsidising the buyers of new HDB flats and this is one of the many matters discussed in our Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The current deficits are fully budgeted and paid for each year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Under PSP's proposal, though, the initial Government subsidy will be even higher.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The cost of building the flat and the cost of land do not change.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The cost of land and cost of building will still be the same.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only difference is the initial income from selling the flats would be less.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this means the initial Government deficit will be very significant when the scheme is launched, which means we will need more taxes to fund it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Subsequently, if and when people sell flats, the Government may get money in fits and starts, but this will be more difficult to properly budget for because we do not know how many people will sell and how much will be earned from this and it will be difficult to predict and plan spending on the basis of income at the time people sell flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, while Mr Leong talks about the importance of affordable and available housing, at the same time, he talks about wanting an exuberant or vibrant resale market for those who want to sell their flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Clearly, if you are being honest, there is a tension between affordability and an exuberant resale market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the resale market is very exuberant, prices would be high.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this is what people who want to sell would want, but this is not what buyers would want.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, many of the buyers at those prices would be unhappy if they see others getting windfalls based on the lottery at the BTO, which will only be exaggerated if we follow Mr Leong's proposal of the low initial sticker price.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If people who buy flats become unable to sell because of the imprisoning effect of a land cost upon sale, then resale prices are likely to spike as the only supply will be those who own older flats not subject to the scheme.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The new flats will have more difficulty coming into the resale market to bring prices down.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will exaggerate the already divergent market between resale flats and BTOs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This would also restrict the additional supply and the resale market leaving prices to spike further in the short-term, which is where we face problems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The PSP also proposes a rental housing scheme with rental houses in prime areas for people who want them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I have no objections to the expansion of a rental scheme, ultimately, this has to be compared to other priorities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: HDB has a limited supply of flats every year and with expanded supplies, the demand at these prices is much higher than the available supply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I therefore believe HDB should continue to prioritise building flats for those who need BTOs first.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And in the event we reach a stage where the demand for BTO flats is adequately abated, we can then consider other priorities such as public housing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the priority for rental housing should still be families in financial difficulty who cannot afford to buy flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also made the argument that the Government should encourage more people to rent rather than own flats, and that this too should be provided by the public sector.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Flat ownership gives every Singaporean a stake in Singapore and its success.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If Singapore enjoys economic growth over a long period of time, homeowners will see home prices rise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By allowing every Singaporean easy access to buy at least one subsidised flat in their life, every Singaporean is assured of some upside in the course of their life, as long as they own a flat and Singapore continues to do well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If one bought a BTO flat and lived in it for five to 10 years and later decided they wanted to move to a different place later, they would at least have enjoyed some upside and have some additional cash when they sell, if they want to move to a new place, assuming Singapore has done well and the resale prices have gone up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if they rented for 10 years, in those 10 years, they would have paid their landlord, perhaps helping their landlord pay their mortgage, while at the same time losing their own opportunity to enjoy the upside from property appreciation at that time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, the flat price Bala's Curve that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim distributed is not an accurate description of how flat prices actually behave in the secondary market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reality is that because of Singapore's economic growth over the decades, even flats bought in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s are selling at well above the prices they were bought for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Alternatively, if they do not wish to sell it, they can pass it on to their children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is likely that towards the end of a flat's lease, likely the last 30 years or so, prices will trend downwards.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is it unfair that prices do not rise forever and eventually come down?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By the time flats get to this stage, it is likely the original owners and several others would have bought and sold it over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those who have not sold their flats but rather lived in the flats, they would have enjoyed living there for more than 60 years or around two generations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a long time to enjoy your home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Those who buy closer to the end of the lease will be able to negotiate a lower price for it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We can see this in the private property market where several private properties are reaching the end of their lives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we talk about $1 million public housing, there are also landed properties available for less than $1 million.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are landed houses in Jalan Chempaka Kuning selling for less than $1 million at the moment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reason is that they have a remaining lease of less than 12 years, yet even these houses have a ready market and transactions are taking place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are people who would like a larger house and are prepared to accept a shorter lease in exchange for a lower price.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the long term, as HDB flats cross the 60-year mark, for example, some would have values drop.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in my view, this would create more options for the secondary housing in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, if people want shorter-lease flats, the only options are 2-room flats for seniors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the coming years, we may have a resale market with cheaper flats on shorter leases for those who prefer larger houses for a shorter period of time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I see many examples of this at my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are families with teenage children who want a larger flat while their children are teens or who have parents moving in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They need it for immediate purposes, but in the longer term, say when seniors pass on or when children grow up, they may want the flexibility to change their housing arrangements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe a housing market that has flats of all sizes at different price points will, ultimately, give all people more options to find a flat that suits their needs in the secondary market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will reduce the crunch on the BTO market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The HDB market is, currently, an anomalous situation because of the slowdown in building that occurred over the last two years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also believe that the spike in demand has been contributed to by the big difference between the HDB resale market and the BTO market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Every buyer would like to buy on the BTO market, and so, they try their luck in the ballot as long as they qualify.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only ones to buy in the resale market are those who have the means and who need a flat urgently.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The MOP is a fair measure for those who obtained subsidised BTO flats or obtained subsidies for purchasing resale flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding my suggestions though, I support Minister Desmond Lee's Motion wholeheartedly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think HDB has done a wonderful job of providing affordable housing for Singaporeans for many generations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The last three years of COVID-19 slowed down flat construction and skewed the queue and waiting time for BTOs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I support the plans to expand and catch up on the building of flats and hope that this will help to ameliorate the real pain point at the moment, which is the supply crunch of BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think we can, or should, break the system as suggested by the Progress Singapore Party and the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In accordance with the decision of this House to have a simultaneous debate on both Motions, I will now call on Members to make their speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are allowed to consider both Motions in a single speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The first part of my speech will touch on the overarching principles and values that should guide our housing policy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the early years of our Independence, HDB flats were built for rental and then later for sale primarily as an affordable home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But today many younger Singaporeans feel that the Singapore dream of a HDB flat is increasingly out of reach, or at least, severely challenging.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I spoke to a young Singaporean recently who will be marrying this year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She tried and failed twice to get a Built-To-Order (BTO) flat in a non-mature estate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given this, as well as the time factor, she is now looking at resale options, but resale prices are high.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On top of the price, the cash plus the CPF upfront component that they need to pay to get a bank mortgage loan, or even a HDB loan is substantial.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Both of them are young and have little CPF savings, so they have to seek funding from their parents, who have their own difficulties to cope with, or find other solutions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And that feeling is coupled with another – the high price of resale flat, which keeps getting higher.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The generation that grew up during the heyday of the asset appreciation approach to policy have grown up with the expectation that HDB prices will keep on rising and that this is very, very good.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But one simple truth is dawning on more and more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If HDB flat prices rise and rise, that inevitably tends to affect our house prices for the young.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That is because land sale values from the state to HDB seem to be influenced by historical sale transactions and that in turn affects BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The fiscal capacity of the state to provide subsidies out of the Budget is not unlimited.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, the HDB flat lessee may realise some capital gain, but his or her children may be struggling in the housing market.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The passing of the years in generational change has made more and more Singaporeans grasp this fundamental reality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is another fundamental reality that has not been fully grasped and that is that the resale prices of flats will inevitably hit a point when it starts to decline.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many of us are not so focused on this lease decay issue right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With the HDB resale market buoyant, it can seem like it is not relevant to the time that we are living in.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it is something Singapore will have to contend with the medium to longer term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Stocks and shares have generally risen over the long term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: HDB flats are not like stocks and shares.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Framing policies, setting expectations that the price of a flat is going to go up and up and up, and never come down, is not sustainable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Older HDB lessees can see this when their children start to enter the housing market.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are two other reasons to reboot our mindset and move away from the mental model of the HDB flat as an ever-appreciating asset that uplifts generations through property price uplift.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, if we frame our policies to prompt rising resale values in the belief that monetising that resale value should be one of the main ways we provide for retirement, where does that leave those who do not want to sell and move out?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many elderly Singaporeans are living in flats worth a considerable sum, but they do not want to downgrade.
