speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some want to stay put in the communities where they have sunk roots, where their friends and relatives are, where they have social capital, where they are familiar with the neighbourhood and its hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Others may look around at the market for buying a smaller home and find that after deducting brokers' commission, renovation and moving costs, and after factoring in the need to repay CPF accrued interest which more and more sellers are finding that they cannot do, the prospect of downgrading does not release enough cash for the upside to outweigh the downside.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Plus, most are unwilling to take up the Lease Buyback Scheme, as most probably they want to leave their flat to their children, who they think will face even higher property prices in the future, which probably explains the scheme's low take-up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many are unwilling or unable to rent out their flats for reasons of privacy or not having alternative dwellings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But when greater rewards can be gotten from gaming the property market and flipping properties, the urge to do those other things lessens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The expectation of ever-rising property prices can become the opiate of the masses, depleting our entrepreneurial and innovative impulses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And Singaporeans will get a better and more sustainable uplift if all our minds are focused instead on nurturing an economy that creates better-paying future-proof jobs with a decent career path, including vocational ones and combine that with some degree of national redistribution to offset advantages of birth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is this asset appreciation assumption still the centre of gravity of our housing policy?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are various statements from the Government on this, and some seem, on the face of it, to be contradictory.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There have been statements that prices may keep on rising even after year 70, for example from former Ministry of National Development Minister Khaw Boon Wan in September 2018.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And there was Deputy Prime Minister Mr Lawrence Wong's statement in 2017 that resale prices will eventually come down to zero as the lease decays.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will not quote the various statements that could be quoted, due to time limitations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What in Government policy-making is the boundary line that divides affordability from unaffordability on a metric of housing affordability?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One widely used housing portability metric is the median multiple or house-price-to-income ratio.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This indicator was a primary indicator of the 1991 World Bank UNCHS housing indicator system and was used as a measure of how affordability by the UN Commission for Sustainable Development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Its use has been publicised by an organisation called Demographia which studies housing affordability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Demographia views a multiple 5.1 as severely unaffordable, 4.1 to 5 is seriously unaffordable, 3.14 is moderately unaffordable and under 3 is affordable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Parliamentary colleague, Sengkang Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua, filed a Parliamentary Question to obtain data as regards HPI for first timers who bought resale HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For those who bought BTO flats ranged from 4.8 to 2.9.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At this point, Sir, I note that the hon Member Xie Yao Quan referred to our 2020 manifesto formula which called for a maximum debt-service ratio selling price for HDB BTO flats in non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This cap to the debt-service ratio applies to all flat types, including 5-room BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are other elements in the formulation, such as a cap to loan tenure and further discounts for 2- to 3-roomed flats in that manifesto formulation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Xie's example compares median 4-room BTO flats in non-mature estates to our maximum cap.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our position now of three, or close to three HPI for BTO in non-mature estates that my hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim explained is developed based on new information derived that my hon friend, Sengkang Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua, from his Parliamentary Question, that first-time applicants collecting keys for BTO flats had a median household income of $7,700 per month.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We believe that it is useful to refocus the conversation on first-timer median income, not national household median income.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, the Workers' Party view that we should aim for HPI of three or close to three for non-mature BTOs as a function of first-timer household income.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does it view, for example, anything under an HPI level of six as affordable, or HPI level of five as affordable?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To be sure, I am not saying that the Government should accept the Demographia classification, but the Government should clarify what its stance on the HPI is.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My third question is on planning sufficient supply of HDB flats for new household startups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, the rate of formation of new households as a result of marriages, or even other kinds of events like divorces, is not something that changes drastically from year to year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is demographic data that does not see sudden or radical changes in general.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government controls most of the land in Singapore and hence, does not face impediments in terms of being able to acquire land to build HDB flats, unlike in many countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why then do we get into situations where the supply of HDB BTO flats cannot keep up with demand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Where there is excess demand such that BTO projects are oversubscribed at increasing ratios as my hon friend, Louis Chua, has expanded on in detail and much demand that would go to BTOs ends up going instead into the resale market leading to resale price spikes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not just due to COVID-19 delays.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This happened in the pre-COVID-19 past, too, at times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful if the Government can share its perspective on this and also share what it does to research and plan ahead to match supply with demand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My fourth and last question to the Government is on the link between housing and our total fertility rate, or TFR.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is often said that economic factors like house price are not the only factor affecting the willingness of couples to have children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Talking to many of my constituents in Serangoon ward and Aljunied GRC and fellow Singaporeans over the years, I am of the view that while not being the only factor, it is a very important factor indeed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I recently spoke to a constituent in Serangoon.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Both the husband and wife are university graduates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Surveying their housing options, she felt that the burden of debt to acquire a decent home was so high that they were unsure as to whether to bring children into the world if they did not have the economic means to give their children all the support they would need to thrive in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Government if it takes seriously the possible linkage between TFR and housing access and affordability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Has it studied the effect of rising and high house prices on our TFR?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Surely, this is a question that can be addressed through economic modelling, regression analysis and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government studied this and shared data on this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If it has not studied, would it do so?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to the third and last part of my speech where I will share two concrete suggestions to improve accessibility and affordability for HDB housing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This will allow BTO flats to be sold at a lower price.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such flats may also will better suit the life plans of many buyers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, someone aged 50 may buy such a 70-year-lease flat at year 20 because they want a shorter lease and they do not expect to live beyond 100, or those who may want to stay in the same flat for life may also find this attractive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would be another addition to the HDB ecosystem that widens choice to Singaporeans who may want very different things at different stages in their lives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this proposal, payment for the optional additional 29-year period is made only upon the exercising the option, but the option payment is locked in from the day of the initial purchase.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This option should be exercised not later than five years before expiry of the initial lease period.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That cheaper price may make possible a shorter loan duration, which many would welcome as being less risky, given the vicissitudes of life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The CPF funds saved thereby would get compounded in the buyer's CPF accounts and boost retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The state can take back the flat upon lease expiry and it can be put to various uses such as public rental housing or Sale of Balance Flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The assumptions and principles behind this new 70+29 BTO flat have some parallels with those behind the Lease Buyback Scheme, which allows leases to be shortened, with some monetary benefit gained for the lessee.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The core idea in this proposal is actually mooted in this House by my hon friend and Member of Parliament for Sengkang Louis Chua at MND's Committee of Supply last year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is this a reasonable expectation for our society to have of newlyweds and new households starting up?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: During those years of waiting, the couple will have to find other living arrangements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many choose to stay with parents but that does not come without challenges, for obvious reasons – challenges that can strain young families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some would certainly postpone childbearing for this reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Building more flats ahead of demand would create some buffer stock – some redundancy in the system – to allow couples to buy a BTO flat faster without the current wait times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In comments HDB made to CNA in November last year said that it is already building ahead of demand or actual bookings where possible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Since May 2011, it has called for and awarded construction tenders for the majority of BTO projects ahead of the outcome of the flat selection.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My suggestion here is to build more of such advance build BTOs more frequently and to create a special class of flats built ahead of demand as another complementary plank in our HDB ecosystem once market conditions have become normalised from what they are today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These would be flats where there is no requirement to sell before construction starts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One objection to this proposal is what if the flats remain unsold for a long time?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The cost of maintaining those empty flats would be a loss to the state.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, if such flats remain unsold, the selling price could be reduced until we reach a market clearing level where someone will buy – which is how markets operate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The risk of flats remaining permanently unsold is small once you consider this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, HDB would obviously conduct market research before deciding to build certain flat types in certain locations, which would lower that risk even more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Unsold flats could also be repurposed for the expanded public rental stock as proposed by my colleague and Member of Parliament for Sengkang Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not calling for all flats to be built this way – only some.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we can build industrial facilities ahead of demand, can we not also build residential homes ahead of demand to reduce the wait time for new couples to encourage faster new household formation and perhaps childbearing to lift our globally abysmal total fertility rate (TFR)?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I should note that I am suggesting building this new class of built-in-advance flats after we have cleared the we have cleared the current BTO backlog so as not to divert resources away from that task, though planning for that should start early.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Just to recap, the Workers' Party's manifesto in 2020 said, and I quote, "HDB BTO selling prices in non-mature estates should be based on a 20-year mortgage, 10% downpayment and monthly repayment of a maximum of 25% of the median monthly household income." So, it is pegged to the median household income.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If I heard Mr Leon Perera correctly just now, the Workers' Party's position is that they should apply to all flats, including 5-room flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is not an expression of a target for the average.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our formulation also has other elements in it, which differ from typical transactions right now – a 20-year loan tenure, 10% downpayment and additional subsidies for 2- and 3-room flats to lower the eventual BTO selling price even more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, yes, it applies to all flats – that position in the manifesto, but it is a maximum cap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: So, if I hear him correctly, the Workers' Party was suggesting in its manifesto, offering a definition of affordability.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: That definition is based on median household income applied to all flat types, including 5-room flats, when we know that HDB flats cater to the whole range of Singaporeans up to the 80th income percentile.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: So, the Workers' Party's position is basically to peg the definition of affordability to median household income, even for higher-income earners in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As I mentioned to Mr Xie, that formulation was a maximum cap, not the expression of where the average should be targeted at.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I am not sure I fully understand his question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I would like to ask Mr Xie what is the point that he is trying to make and also, I would like to ask Mr Xie what is his view on affordability?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: At what level of HPI between what is affordable and what is not affordable?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Well, Sir, I think the point is this that according to Mr Perera's clarification, the Workers' Party's proposition of pegging the highest flat type – a 5-room – to median income, basically must mean that the cost of a 5-room flat for higher-income Singaporeans must come down.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I think it is reasonable to assume that a proposal to peg housing price to median income must be based on a median flat type.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: If Mr Perera is proposing that the highest flat type must also be pegged to median income, then I would like to ask Mr Perera just how exactly does he suggest funding this – because it must mean that the price of a 5-room flat must come down to a median income level.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As I clarified several times, I am not sure why there seems to be a disconnect here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That formulation in the Workers' Party's 2020 manifesto was a maximum cap for 5-room flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is a cap that comes about by way of capping the debt service ratio at 25%.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Then, you work out a price based on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are other elements in that formulation as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The prices of other types of flats would follow correspondingly from that maximum cap which would probably apply for a 5-room BTO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To address his question on funding, if you listen to the proposals that we are making in this debate in totality, we have spoken to that question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We have spoken, for example, about the approach to land valuation that can be taken.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I think we have got proposals that addressed how these things are going to be funded.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I would remind Mr Xie again that our position is aiming to three or close to three HPI for BTO in a non-mature estate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I have another question for Mr Xie as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does Mr Xie Yao Quan acknowledge that if we have a mental model of ever appreciating house prices and then we have a model of valuing land based on comparables and historicals, the tail is wagging the dog?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We will get an escalation of prices going on for a long, long time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That will mean that if we want to keep BTO prices stable, we have to increase subsidies more and more and more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: This is something that is useful that has come up and I think we can debate on that.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: But to Mr Perera's question, I agree with the Minister that our housing prices for non-mature estate BTOs are affordable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: You are saying that the current HPI for BTOs – you feel that this is affordable, basically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, where does Mr Xie think the money is going to come from?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Murali Pillai, do you have any clarifications?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I thought I would be outstaying your welcome by asking.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Both of them have outstayed their welcome, not you.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Just a short clarification for the hon Member Leon Perera.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He mentioned that one of the reasons people do not want to use the Lease Buyback Scheme was because they want to fund the purchase for their children's flat.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One of the major drivers is that these people would find that their retirement needs are met and therefore they do not need to enter into Lease Buyback arrangements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This was referenced in the Workers' Party "HDB Reforms" paper.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We had a section of it where we talked about what is the available evidence at the time the paper was written – which was November 2022.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, what is the available academic evidence out there were the reasons why the take-up rate for the LBS has been so low.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In other words, not everyone is able to monetise their flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, if we build an ecosystem of policies where monetising your flat – because the price is high and appreciating – monetising your flat is going to be one of the key planks of retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Those people who want to keep the flat for their children, those people who do not want to tap on LBS, do not want to rent out their flat, will not be able to benefit from that plank of retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, that was the point of my speech.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have considered very carefully the motions put up by the hon Members Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa, which I will refer to as the “PSP Motion”; and that put up by the hon Minister for National Development, which I will refer to as the “Government’s Motion”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The points raised in the PSP Motion are, in my view, raising correct objectives for public housing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Affordable and accessible public housing, preserving the owner-occupant nature of it, ensuring that retirees have access to public housing and keeping it inclusive are all ingredients of a successful public housing policy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The PSP Motion calls for a review of policy is also not objectionable – government policies should be reviewed from time to time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The operative two words in the PSM Motion is “in order”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I quote: “That this House calls upon the Government to review its public housing policies in order to deliver affordable and accessible HDB flats”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The use of the words “in order” suggests that existing policies do not deliver the objectives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While I agree that certain aspects of Government policies should be reviewed, I simply cannot agree that current policies do not aim to provide accessible and affordable housing or that they do not look at providing for retirees and so on.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, even a cursory review of public housing policies would show that all of the points raised in the PSP Motion are actually explicitly stated objectives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will elaborate on why I disagree with this.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will therefore support the Government’s Motion but I would also like to make several observations and suggestions on public housing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My first point is that affordable public housing should not be seen as cheap public housing and that accessible public housing does not mean that everyone will be able to get a flat in their choice location at the time that that may want it, devoid of other considerations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As a small country with land scarcity, high level of development and general affluence of our population, we cannot expect that property prices would be anything else than fairly pricey.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And this will be so whether it is public housing or private housing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Affordability and accessibility should be created by Government policies like grants, the provision of HDB loans, where possible, waivers of certain requirements and flexibility in imposing eligibility criteria, for example.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Accessibility is also created by varying, amongst other things, lease tenure and limiting certain types of flat to only certain categories of buyers, like flats for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My second point is that public housing has to go beyond just affordability and accessibility.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, public housing policies are not merely about bricks and mortar and the cost of flats, but it is also a set of social policies that aims to achieve various objectives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As the hon Minister said when launching the scheme, without Government intention, only the well-to-do would be able to afford housing in attractive locations and that the Government was determined not to let such stratification and segregation happen, as it has successful cities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, to ensure inclusivity, rental flats would also be built within these prime estates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, thought had obviously been put in such that while pursuing the objective of inclusivity, other undesirable consequences do not inadvertently arise.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But another aspect that public housing policy as a social policy should take into consideration, is how to give effect to the aspirations of Singaporeans for upgrading.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As we all know, Singaporeans have an almost innate desire for upgrading our property as we earn more and as our families grow larger.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, it is also important to create opportunities for upgrading within the public housing milieu, including the possibility of upgrading by getting a bigger flat or a flat in a better location.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my third point – that HDB must continue to show value to buyers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even as I say that prices of public housing will continue to rise due Singapore’s characteristics, HDB should continually look to building and selling flats of a high quality and also of diverse types to cater for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Location Scheme was one such example that I had raised.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In Punggol, there are beautiful, new seafront flats, of which I am sure view is absolutely amazing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a need to accommodate the elderly, which includes downgraders – silver Singaporeans who wish to downgrade from their private properties or larger flats, as their children move out or as their mobility is reduced.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Singles are another group and many not look not to buying just small two room flats, but larger flats as they may wish to also house their parents or to just have more space for lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: HDB must look into all of these aspirations – from the practical like ageing and retirement to the aspirational like upgrading and lifestyle; and for some, the desire for a fantastic view.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This must be so, because our public housing cannot be, like in other countries, basic.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: With 80% of our population living in public housing, it is a diverse group with a range of income, priorities and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My next point is to caution about generalising about public housing, based on a few cases or news reports.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: An example is the increasing number of flats being sold above $1 million in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at these flats, they have a particular nature.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is that of the flat being put up for sale without the buyer having ever occupied it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Based on what the Ministry and HDB has said, these are rare cases of abuse and there are penalties that can be applied to such incidences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One swallow does not make it spring and these outliers do not mean the public housing system has failed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There will always be people who will try their luck at these things.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What is important is that they are caught and they are brought to task.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The idea is that if these buyers occupy the flats for their entire lives, that they would essentially never have to pay for the land cost, and that this would make flats affordable at the outset.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me say that I imagine that this proposal arises from Mr Leong’s fixation with land cost and his fixation with the payment made by the Government to the state as consideration for state land.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we recall Mr Leong’s earlier proposal in December, it was that, and I quote “Land costs should be take out of the picture”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He had also proposed that HDB flat prices should account only for construction costs and price differences between locations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Leong had also separately suggested that land could be sold at historical rates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Leong now makes a different proposal – that the land cost be paid only when the flat is sold.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, it appears that he has accepted the Minister’s explanation that land cost should, in fact, be “part of the picture”, as it were, but that payment for it should be kicked down the road, albeit with interest.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, if it is a matter of the Government purchasing the land first but not charging it when it sells the flat, it means that the Government will become a de facto creditor to all persons living in HDB flats who have not sold their property.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And the question arises whether the Government should be essentially lending money to citizens in this way.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it means that when a person sells their flat, they may be left with nothing or even a deficit – because interest continues to run as long as they live in the flat.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, their debt to the Government actually grows larger over time and this could become a disincentive to remain in the flat.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Related to this is what is the rate that interest should be fixed at – because anything lower than the fair market rate would mean that the Government is being deprived of a certain amount of money that could be used for expenditure in other areas that could benefit a larger number of people.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, even if a person lives in the flat for his whole life, he is unlikely to live longer than the period of the 99-year lease.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What then would happen when he passed away?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Is the cost of the land to be borne by the purchaser, the inheritor, or will the land cost merely disappear?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: All these questions arise, of course, in a model where the Government pays the state for the land first, then sells the flats once they are built on the basis of the proposed scheme.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, it appears that Mr Leong is actually suggesting that the state not be paid first but only once the buyer sells his flat.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Because Mr Leong mentioned that the payment would be made back into the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is simply wrong and it is not the way that the reserves work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, although Mr Leong started his speech by saying that he would like to propose a reset of housing policies, in fact, Mr Leong is proposing a reset of much more, including the entire system of how our reserves are maintained and managed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He is proposing to turn the system that has underpinned our financial stability on its head.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But, Sir, arising from these Motions, this debate and the various proposals by Mr Leong, is a larger question of democratic accountability and the nature of politics and political debate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Over the Chinese New Year period, while chatting with friends at gatherings, this issue of public housing and land costs came up more than once.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I was disappointed when some of my friends and relatives said that, well, paying for state land is simply a matter of left pocket, right pocket; and that Mr Leong’s original proposal of excluding land costs would make sense.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This, Sir, is a sad instance of where something incorrect is repeated oft enough, it becomes to believed to be the truth.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But coming back to these Chinese New Year gatherings, I took pains to explain to them that this is not a matter of left pocket, right pocket.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, it is a matter of two completely pairs of trousers worn by two completely different people.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Minister had given his explanation on precisely this last month.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For me, it is intuitive, because many years ago, I worked in the Singapore Land Authority, in the land sales department.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But what is the reality of how it will be received by the public?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But it will create confusion and misunderstanding of Government policies and it will create unreasonable expectations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This, Sir, of course, is a larger question of how we want our politics to evolve, what is the level of democratic accountability we expect, whether there can be some sharing of the burden of responsibility, to increase accountability and the accessibility to information.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Coming back to these Motions, Sir, many of our policies are finely calibrated and work in tandem with each other.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I stand in support of the Government’s Motion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The original mission behind the Housing and Development Board (HDB) when it was set up in 1960 was to alleviate the severe housing shortage at that time by building affordable homes for the population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in 1989, public housing flats took on another role as an appreciating asset for their lessees when the Government announced several major policy changes with regard to HDB resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the income ceiling for the purchase of resale flats was removed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This allowed people to buy HDB flats even if they were higher-income earners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, Permanent Residents (PRs) were allowed to buy HDB resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This supported the Government's liberalisation of immigration policies to attract more middle- and higher-income foreigners to come to work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And third, HDB flat owners were allowed to purchase private property for investment purposes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These measures added liquidity to the public housing market which pushed up prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government also introduced various upgrading programmes for HDB flats and estates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In addition to improving the living environment of HDB flat dwellers, this also bolstered the view that HDB flats are an appreciating asset.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Flat upgrading was pitched to voters by the PAP during the 1997 General Elections (GE) as a benefit they would enjoy priority for if their precincts voted for PAP candidates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Voters were told that after upgrading, their flats will increase in value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Conversely, precincts that voted for the Opposition risk being placed further back in the upgrading queue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Soon after the 1997 GE, then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong assessed that linking the upgrading programme to electoral support was the single most important factor in the vote swing to the PAP and that it was decisive in tipping floating voters in the PAP's favour.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Hougang and Potong Pasir voters did not bite the carrot offered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, by 2015, Opposition-held wards like Hougang eventually started getting their lifts and flats upgraded.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The scheme lost its effectiveness as a political tool.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, in my conversations with many residents in Hougang, it was this perceived unfairness that prompted them to vote against the PAP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is natural for people to not just desire a home to live in, but also to own an asset which grows in value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many people think that their salaries alone will not make them rich.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Properties, including HDB flats, are seen as very attractive assets to grow one's wealth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For the first two decades of the Government's asset-enhancement policy, the property asset drive mindset worked like a charm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many HDB lessees saw eye-watering increases in their property wealth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this pathway to wealth requires ever-increasing property prices to sustain it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Every property bought would need to be sold for significantly more than the purchase price.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those who bought HDB flats in the 1980s and 1990s may be glad to see that their properties have increased in value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, to unlock the value of these assets, they will need to sell and downgrade their properties before their leases start to decay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those with adult children would realise that the situation is much more precarious for their offspring.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many parents of young adults nowadays worry that their young children may not be able to realise the same dream they themselves achieved to own a home of their own.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those who are better off had gone ahead and bought properties for their children to move in when they get married.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others have migrated to Australia, New Zealand and Canada, where they are able to buy landed property for the price of an HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But where does that leave the rest of Singaporeans who do not have wealthy parents and want to remain in this country to build their homes, careers and families?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While many who graduated in the 1970s were able to afford a landed home after a few years of work, private properties are now out of the question for most younger graduates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even resale flats are now out of reach for many of them, leaving BTO flats the only remaining option.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My hon friends Louis Chua, Leon Perera and Jamus Lim have tabled proposals on making the price of BTO flats more affordable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the remainder of my speech, I will focus on moderating the price of resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many young couples buying their first flat prefer to live near their parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This provides them the familiar surroundings that they grew up in and the companionship they can offer to their parents and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their parents are also able to help care for their children when they are at work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many home buyers also prefer living in mature estates were amenities and transport links to the city are better developed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Only resale flats can meet many of these requirements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is also why BTO flats in mature estates are so popular.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of my residents have approached me to ask me for help to appeal to HDB for priority to get a BTO or Sale of Balance Flat in a mature estate, after trying many times to secure one in balloting exercises and failing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When I suggest using a resale flat and using Government grants to help with the downpayment, my suggestion is often met with great scepticism, because resale flat prices feel so far out of reach for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This ratio is the resale flat price divided by the household income of the buyers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to the International Housing Affordability ratings by Demographia, such a median multiple would be rated as "seriously unaffordable".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The median multiple would need to be 3.0 and under to be considered affordable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This has pushed many of my residents to either rent at high open market rates or compete with other home buyers to ballot for BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to moderate the growth in resale flat prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our goal must be to moderate the growth, not to make the prices collapse, because the latter would negatively affect many existing flat lessees who are depending on their flats as a source of future retirement income.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are two ways to moderate resale flat price growth without imposing price caps by government fiat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are: to reduce demand and to increase the supply of resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has already introduced the 15-month waiting out period for private property downgraders to reduce demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will focus on measures to increase the supply of HDB resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is potentially a large stock of HDB resale flats that can be put on the market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many seniors live in flats that are larger than what they require after their children have gotten married and moved out.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It becomes difficult for them to clean and maintain such a large flat on their own.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These flats could potentially be sold on the resale market if their owners are prepared to move into new 2-room Flexi flats on short-term leases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of these 2-room flats come with elderly-friendly fittings and nearby amenities, which seniors find quite attractive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, not all elderly applicants for 2-room Flexi flats are successful.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If a larger proportion of the 71,000 senior households decided to sell their flats and buy 2-room Flexi flats, the demand will far outstrip supply.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By 2030, 25% of our population will be over 65.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The number in need right-sized flats will only grow as the years go by.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government needs to provide more help to seniors who wish to right-size their flats by building more 2-room Flexi flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Doing so will have the twin benefit of increasing the supply of resale flats for new hone buyers and moderating their prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Another area that the Government should look into to increase the supply of resale flats is to prospectively restrict the concurrent ownership of HDB and private property.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, private property owners who want to buy an HDB flat are required to dispose of their property before buying an HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has stated that this is to prioritise our limited supply of public housing for residents who do not own other properties.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the reverse is not true – HDB flat owners are allowed to buy private residential property without selling their HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can do so if they meet the Minimum Occupation Period and pay the Additional Buyer Stamp Duty (ABSD) of at least 17% on the purchase of their second and subsequent residential property.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has stated that this is allowed because HDB recognises that the financial position of HDB flat owners may improve over time and some may aspire to own private residential property.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I acknowledge that this is a valid aspiration of many higher-income Singaporeans, realising this aspiration cannot come at the expense of less well-off Singaporeans who are only looking for a roof over their heads.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Of these, 45% are not living in their flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, there are about 15,000 HDB units which are not occupied by their owners who live in another private property that they own.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This represents a not insignificant number of HDB flats that could potentially add to the resale flat supply and moderate the price of resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I do acknowledge that many of these flats are rented out, adding to the supply of open market rental flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government given further consideration to the possibility of future buyers of private properties being required to sell their HDB flats?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When I asked the Minister for National Development in November last year, he said that the Government has been "gathering views from Singaporeans as part of Forward Singapore and will study these as well as other views and ideas carefully".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If this policy is implemented prospectively, it will not immediately add to the supply of resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in the medium to long-term, it will better promote the owner-occupation intent of public housing and better ensure an adequate supply of affordable resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's public housing policies were a great success in the first few decades after our independence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But the Government got distracted along the way when it started pairing the objective of affordable housing with that of asset enhancement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a result, public housing has become unaffordable by some international measures.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of 2020, I began my own journey in looking for a flat of my own to start a family.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It was admittedly an exciting time when we looked at all the factors and options we could consider in the public housing domain.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There were many factors we had to consider: Should we stay in a mature or non-mature estate?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Who will help when we have kids in the future?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Will it make a difference if we do not have a car?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Is the opportunity cost of time due to longer travelling times, for example, be taken into account if we settle for a further location?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Will this be our forever home or will it be a stepping stone to something else?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: To complicate things further, due to the effects of the pandemic, there were BTO project delays, which resulted in the rise of resale flat prices.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It did make us jittery to see the price going up month on month the longer we took to make a decision.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Buying house is one of the biggest purchases a young couple can make.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For me at least, it shone a spotlight on the role of HDB and how has it evolved over the years.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And more importantly, moving forward, how will it be in the future?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The last few years have seen many significant and rapid changes to the housing landscape.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on supply chain and manpower disruptions have driven up the price of resale flats for the eleventh consecutive quarter as people look for quicker alternatives.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is a concern, especially for those who cannot qualify for BTOs and ECs but are unable to afford private property.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In the recent October sitting in 2022, I had asked about the number of HDB homeowners who have purchased a second private property.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the strong demand in public housing and the high resale prices, will the Government consider HDB flat owners to sell their flats when they purchase a private property to free up more flats moving forward?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, we can prioritise couples and families who need a house.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They are subject to an income cap of $16,000.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I did a quick check on the DBS home loan website.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For couple who is a first-timer with a combined income of $16,000 which is the cap looking to buy an EC, based on the indicative prevailing interest rates of 3% to 4.25% and the maximum loan period of 30 years, the couple will be eligible for a loan of up to $975,000 and affordability-wise to purchase a property worth $1.3 million.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, if we were to take a look at the recently launched Tenet EC, the units actually range between $1.1 to 2.1 million.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the HDB grants, it may still be challenging for the couple to afford the larger unit with a combined income of $16,000.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, would the Government consider reassessing the income caps for executive condominiums?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, how can we overcome BTO construction delays and be resilient against such supply chain and manpower disruption in the future?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: HDB taken a bold step forward by embracing new technologies that can accelerate construction and completion times.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is promising and paves the way for looking at technology which can create a more resilient construction industry.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I commend them on going on this path of research, innovation and hope this can continue.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to see how the policies have continuously evolved to ensure accessibility and affordability.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The curated shared life experiences in HDBs for social cohesion and diversity are unmatched anywhere else in the world.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Thank you, Mr Speaker, for giving me this opportunity to speak.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Having heard the debate yesterday and comments on social media, especially after having heard the speeches of Progress Singapore Party (PSP) Members of Parliament, I feel that I should say a few words.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: First, yesterday, Member of Parliament Hazel Poa asked why we could not build sufficient flats in one go, like what we have done during Mr Lee Kuan Yew's time.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: She also asked the Minister whether he thought Mr Lee Kuan Yew had raided our reserves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: At that time, we didn’t have a mature HDB resale market, nor did we have much reserves to speak of.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What was the point or purpose of her question?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Second, Mr Leong Mun Wai had also spoken about PSP's Affordable Homes Scheme, the purpose of which is to strengthen the principle that a HDB flat is for owner occupation, not investment.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, when he responded to a netizen's comment on his Facebook, he said that his intention was for Singaporeans to keep their CPF money, and not to be "condemned to living in HDB flats" forever because they cannot afford private housing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When I read this, I was very puzzled.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What did he mean by saying "condemned to living in HDB flats"?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, more than 80% of our citizens live in HDB flats and many of them have been living there for their whole life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We bring up our children in HDB flats and some of us have upgraded from a 3-room flat to a 5-room flat.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many middle-income families are very proud of this.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai really should not say that people are "condemned" to stay in HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What is wrong with staying in a HDB flat?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: By saying so, Mr Leong seems to be subconsciously looking down on those who live in HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Since December last year, Mr Leong has kept on changing his stance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Shifting stances aside, I tried to give serious thought to his proposal.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Leong suggested that when selling new flats, the price should only include building cost, thus reducing the price drastically.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Looking at the BTO application data last year and considering our "kiasu" mentality, the PSP proposal will only cause more people to apply for BTO flats, because it is a good deal!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But the resale market will suffer from lack of buyers, the resale price will fall precipitously.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can Mr Leong be sure that such a scenario will not happen?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If this were to happen, the asset value of current HDB flat owners will fall.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How is Mr Leong going to resolve this?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In my constituency in Yishun, there are many Ah Gong and Ah Ma in their 70s or 80s who are thinking of leaving their flat to their children, or selling it and distributing the proceeds to their children, or selling it back to the Government at market price.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, they will not only be able to stay in the same flat, but also have spare money to spend for the rest of their life, without the need to depend on their children so much.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If we were to implement the PSP's policy, Ah Gong and Ah Ma's asset value will drop sharply.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Where then can they get their retirement security?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I can understand the anxieties our residents have been feeling in the past two years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Geopolitical uncertainty, rising prices and the pandemic have made young people, who were forced to stay at home, to want to have their own space more urgently.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Construction delay has also made the younger generation worry about if they are able to get a flat.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: All these anxieties add up to the challenges in getting a flat successfully.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is human nature to feel this way.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, if we look further, these feelings are all transitory and caused by the special circumstances in the past two years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot step on the brake suddenly on the government policies and simply reset.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Now the PSP is calling for a policy reset and its proposals are only for immediate convenience, hoodwinking the people with short-term interests.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Their so-called policy reforms on retirement security are likely to cause 80% of Singaporeans who own HDB flats to lose their safety net overnight.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to address the immediate challenges with right solutions, not empty theories on paper.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge Singaporeans to think over this thoroughly and not try to make hasty changes to important policies because of temporary challenges.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Hasty actions will only lead to our forefathers’ efforts being wasted away.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Motion raised by the Minister for National Development, Mr Desmond Lee.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.14 pm until 4.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because before the break, two Members made certain allegations about my proposals and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I think I have to make a clarification.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Before the break, the Member Ms Carrie Tan made a speech questioning my stance on land cost and public housing policies that I had discussed on social media.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Member Mr Raj Joshua Thomas also referred to the same.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It should be quite clear from this, that I have not called for HDB prices to be based on the historical cost of land.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I have just read out is not inconsistent with what I proposed in the Affordable Homes Scheme (AHS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: She has taken the quote totally out of context.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I was trying to explain to a Facebook comment which said that AHS will condemn Singaporeans to a life in HDB flats – to which I replied that that is not the case because AHS will actually give Singaporeans the opportunity to upgrade, because under AHS, Singaporeans would have more CPF savings in their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If anyone has taken offence by my choice of language, I retract the use of that word, but the quote that Ms Tan has taken, is out of context.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure it is reassuring for people to know that he does not look down on Singaporeans who live in HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But I just want to offer a clarification in response, is that when I read the response and the question posed by the member of public, in the member of public's words, he was concerned about whether the Affordable Homes Scheme (AHS) proposed by Mr Leong would keep citizens stuck in a particular type of housing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And that was the exact word that the citizen said in the Facebook comments.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But it was Mr Leong who responded with the word "condemned", so that is all I wanted to clarify.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, are you making a clarification?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Just now, Member Ms Carrie Tan asked me what is the point of talking about reserves when there were not any at that time?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Several Ministers have educated the House many times on this.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Member Ms Carrie Tan not agree with this?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe all Singaporeans want housing to be affordable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That has always been the commitment of the People's Action Party (PAP) Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The PAP Government has committed that they will price new flats at affordable prices, so that Singaporeans are able to provide for a roof over their heads when they want to start a family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The way that they have done so is through the sale of Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If we look at the prices of BTO flats in the non-mature estates, many of the flats sold are indeed affordable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For those who are lower-income, they can opt for a smaller 3-room flat, and in addition, obtain even more generous housing grants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And I have seen many such cases when I refer my residents to HDB during the Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS).

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are actual figures; these are actual facts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And these prices that Minister Desmond Lee had quoted are before the Government grants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When you factor in all the Government grants, then it is within the range of most home buyers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That is the reason why the majority of Singaporeans live in HDB flats which they have bought and which they have lived in.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If HDB flats are not affordable, then simple put, Singaporeans will not be buying these flats as they will be priced out of their budget.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are a few recent developments in my constituency – Dakota Breeze, Dakota One, Dakota Crest and Pine Vista.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Every one of these BTO launches were over-subscribed, even though the prices of the flats in mature estates were priced slightly higher.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, I received many, many appeals from residents asking whether they can get priority for these BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe the reason why these flats are in high demand is because they represent good value-for-money for that location and they are affordable to the applicants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One would not apply for a BTO flat if they feel that they cannot afford it.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In December last year, HDB released a press release to explain that HDB flats are priced with affordability in mind.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They look at household incomes, they look at the selling prices of flats on offer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Despite the media release, there are still people who may not be aware of the way HDB flats are priced.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, it is important that HDB conveys the relevant information to members of the public, so that the public knows that the Government prices the flats so that they are affordable to residents.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I heard Mr Leong Mun Wai's speech yesterday and his proposed Affordable Homes Scheme (AHS) model.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Leong's proposal to charge for land upon sale simply does not make sense to me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He proposes that when the flat owner sells, the owner would be charged for the land costs, presumably at full cost calculated at the time of buying the flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If HDB is not fully pricing for land when selling the flats, then surely, Mr Leong's proposal will result in a much higher charge to the owner when he sells the flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How is the owner supposed to cough up the land costs when he sells the flat?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Surely, he must pass on the costs to the next buyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But then, why would anyone wish to buy the resale flat if they can get a much cheaper flat from HDB, which according to Mr Leong, is construction costs plus a notional location premium?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He did not give any information about how he would price the location premium and whether this would make the flat even more expensive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But it also begs the question, why does PSP want to charge a flat owner for land cost when HDB currently prices its BTO flats based on affordability and they apply significant grants on top of this?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How does that make the flat more affordable for the flat purchaser under the PSP scheme?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Under PSP's proposal, land cost and construction cost are borne entirely by the buyer when he resells – plus interest accrued.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the buyer's children inherit the flat, if they were to decide many years later to sell the flat, they must pay the land cost plus interest charged over many years and perhaps even decades later.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: His children will be inheriting a huge debt as they cannot sell the flat without having to pay the land cost plus accrued interest.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It thus will become a huge liability to the children of the flat owner and no longer an asset.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even charging construction cost plus, to the first buyer is problematic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Construction cost shot up 30% during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that prices of flats may fluctuate wildly, depending on the market conditions for construction.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, while it may seem affordable to the first buyer, it may be even more expensive on the resale market than today.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Because Mr Leong Mun Wai says that his scheme is designed to reduce resale supply and keep resale prices high.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The resale price demanded by the seller will be higher because resale buyers will have to pay construction costs plus land cost, now payable by the flat buyer, plus interest and the profit the home owner wants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: On the Millennial Apartment Scheme – what makes this scheme different from the private sector renting out flats at market rental?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are already such flats located at various parts of the Central Business District (CBD) like the The Sail at Shenton Way.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are currently being rented out by private developers at market cost.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also visit many friends who live in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I paid a visit there and I walked down the river towards Coney Island.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I posted on my Facebook that the flats look absolutely beautiful.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My view, Mdm Deputy Speaker, is that many of these flats are really world-class and well built.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: While Mr Leong Mun Wai may or may not be living in a HDB flat, he should not say that people living in HDB flats are condemned.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I appreciate that Mr Leong Mun Wai made that correction and I want to say that those who live in HDB flats ought to be proud of the flat that they live in because these are really world-class flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I just want one point of clarification to the hon Member Lim Biow Chuan on the speech he just gave.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I may have misheard him but what I heard was that the hon Member Lim said that the very fact that people are buying BTOs proves that it is affordable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If it is not affordable, they would not be buying it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would the Member agree that there are certain people who have to find a home because living with their parents is not necessarily an option, for various reasons?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would the Member also acknowledge that the concept of housing affordability is a concept in economics that is debated among economists on the understanding that there can be certain levels of house price that are too high in the sense that they crowd out other expenditures that one needs to make in life that are necessary for, for example, education and other things, and that —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, I think you have asked your clarification.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If you cannot afford to buy a car, you do not go and buy a car.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If HDB flats are not affordable, simply put, people will say that, "well, I will find other options.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: In many parts of the world, people do not buy flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: They rent a flat because it is unaffordable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If you look at the countries around the world where home ownership is low, it is because people cannot afford to buy a flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: You look also at the number of subsidies, the grants that the Government gives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Of course, I want to qualify by saying that there will always be that small group of people who for whatever reasons will struggle – because their income is low, because they are not capable of holding onto a good job.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But the Government's commitment to such people is that we will help you.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If you look at those applicants who are living in rental flats, the Government has so many schemes to help you move from that rental flat to buy your own flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I hope Mr Perera will look at the various schemes available, understand how they work and understand that this Government is committed to making flats affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, in response to what Ms Hazel Poa has just said, I am glad that PSP is now acknowledging the fact that the state land is also part of our reserves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: They said that the purpose of their Affordable Homes Scheme is to strengthen the principle of owner occupation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So, what PSP is promoting is that once you buy a HDB flat, you should live there until the end.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Say someone lives in the flat until he reaches the end of his life, what is this person going to do with the flat?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Is he supposed to sell the flat back to the Government and pay back the land cost together with interests?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Take the example of an Ah Gong or Ah Ma in his or her 70s or 80s, who is no longer able to work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: If he or she has to sell the flat back to the Government and pay back the land cost with interests, is he or she not going to leave a large debt to his children?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: No, I am going to reply to Member Ms Tan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In Mandarin):   I Thank Ms Carrie Tan for her query.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In my speech yesterday, I was not able to explain in details the contents of this scheme, so thank you for giving me a chance to clarify this —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, if I could just say, clarify and not make another speech, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: She is asking for me to clarify —

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if his children choose to sell the flat back to HDB, then the selling price will be based on the user price minus the locational premium and some depreciation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: With this formula, they can sell it back to HDB.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many who live in cities, housing-related expenses are the largest share of the wallet.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many home owners around the world, the value of their homes is their largest asset.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That number is an exception in a world where the norm sees homeownership rates across first world countries declining over the last few decades.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Housing policy requires precarious balancing and can sometimes have painful consequences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Adjournment Motion in July 2022, I spoke up for my residents impacted by the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme in Ang Mo Kio towards achieving more equitable outcomes in housing and highlighted the varying difficulties and needs of individual residents, the elderly, in particular, against existing schemes and levies for the Government to consider while attempting to redevelop land in mature estates for future generations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While no housing system in the world is perfect, attempting to brand a system that has allowed for almost nine in 10 Singaporeans to own their homes in a first world city as a failure or malaise, is misleading.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us also not forget that any reset or drastic change proposed for future home owners could affect existing home owners.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we continue to prioritise home ownership over rental?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should Singapore's housing needs continue to be serviced primarily by a public housing model or do we reserve public housing only for the low-income?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there ways to allow for young Singaporeans to start building families earlier?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we improve the quality of life for seniors to age in place?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are all questions I have asked myself, my activists and my residents in the course of my work.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I know countless people in the Civil Service who are kept up at night pondering these questions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Housing policy has not remained stagnant over the years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The work that we do here will ensure that it continues to meet the needs of Singaporeans in the future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My speech will focus on three broad points.
