text: So, how will HDB persuade home buyers that there is a BTO flat for them that is affordable and accessible, rather than for them to hear from coffeeshop talk that HDB flats are not affordable.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe an AI app may help the home buyer to match their needs and budgets to HDB BTO launches as well as resale flats and discover the opportunities that they have not thought of, and that might even save them cost.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Affordability is all about managing your own expectations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number three is that HDB resale prices are driving up BTO prices.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Now, more subsidies for those flats in popular locations, in my opinion will only lead to the BTO flats in these locations being more prize trophies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, putting too much premium for BTO flats in these locations may put it out of reach for ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I think the premium location housing is a good scheme that can be expanded to more popular locales to address this good problem.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number four is the resale prices of HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, the question is whether this is enough to deter speculative behaviour.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And for buyers, do not kill me – I like the idea of the principle of Government sharing in the gains of the resale flats since there were grants involved.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And of course, I like the idea of expanding the PLH rules to cover non-PLH locales and perhaps there can be some form of ABSD or stamp duty when you buy resale.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number five is the current generation of retirees and soon-to-be-retired.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are some Singaporeans who have planned the move to sell their private property or to downsize from the current HDB flat and to retire in a smaller HDB apartment.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Their retirement plans are of course impacted by the cooling measures.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, might the HDB support their efforts to retire well joyfully in a HDB home.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number 6 is now the younger generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In preparing for my speech, I listen to some young people.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is a changing attitude and lifestyle among the younger generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They want more personal space and we have seen more singles moving out of their parents' homes, even when it is a landed property, even when they have their own bedroom, to share a rental flat with friends.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The work-from-home norm which is catching on among the younger generation in particular would require more space at home for work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My advice to them, from my experience working from home should be the flexibility that I can have and not the permanent shift from the employers' real estate costs to my personal real estate expense.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For many of them, they do feel that Government grants are all very helpful, but insufficient BTO and resale prices continue to escalate and the downpayment of 20% is a non-starter unless they get help from their parents.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number seven is the sandwich middle class.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With private condominiums pricing going up, the sandwich middle class hopes that the HDB can raise the income ceiling for HDB's executive condominiums (ECs) and maisonettes so that they may be able to meet their upgrade aspirations at the lower quantum value.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number eight: as HDB is intended to be owner-occupied but the rules allow for them to rent out the HDB flat and live in their private housing, it is good to see the HDB has given our fellow Singaporeans the lift up and the progress to be able to invest in property and, without breaking HDB rules, have the ability to enjoy passive income from renting out their HDB flats most likely to our foreign workforce like nurses, therapists, technician, so on and so forth; all who need affordable rentals place to live.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We read in the news about escalating rentals even for HDB rooms and HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the owners will exercise restraint in the exuberance of profiting from this privilege of having a HDB flat to rent out.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Challenge number nine: notwithstanding that the debate today is around affordability of HDB flats, I would like for us to spend a minute to look at the overall Singapore real estate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In a UBS Global Real Estate Bubble Index Report, it is reported that most households can no longer afford to buy property in the top financial centres of the world without a substantial inheritance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While we do want Singapore to be one of the top global financial hubs, how can we prevent and limit our risk of being in that same situation?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does MAS and MND collectively plan to help ensure that Singaporeans can still get to own our limited residential real estate even as we welcome wealthy family offices into Singapore whose purchasing power will inevitably drive up property sale and rental prices?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is a very tough job and they have created a system that works and is admired.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For all of us in this Chamber, I submit to you that we ought to debate difficult issues in truth and in love.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We should strive to unite and not divide.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We are all here to find solutions that support the integral human development of our society in this small little 724.2 square metres of land.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As Harvard University economist Edward Glaeser once said, "All policies need to be judged by the impact on people." Speaking of people, I would like to share with this House the story of Mdm T told to me by Montford Care, Caritas.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: By the way, all names have been changed to protect the confidentiality of the persons.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One child has a medical condition and the other child is highly active.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They were victims of family violence resulting in Mdm T divorcing the second husband.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: HDB is not only providing affordable homes for Singaporeans, but HDB is taking care of the vulnerable and integrating the resources across the whole-of-Government, MSF and social service agencies to help Singaporeans like Mdm T and her children to have a fresh start in life.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That is the Singapore Spirit, that is the Singapore system.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, indulge me this final quote: “Intentions are not enough – they must be converted into tangible results.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s success is in facilitating results consistent with intentions that are both meaningful and routinely evaluated.” I have faith that we have done it before, and we will do it again.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I stand in support of the Motion in Minister Desmond Lee's name for affordable and accessible public housing, and that this House affirms the importance of keeping public housing affordable and accessible while protecting the interests of current and future generations of Singaporeans and endorses the commitment of the Government to these twin goals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I stand in the support of the Motion raised by hon Member Minister Desmond Lee.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I listen very closely to hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai's Affordable Homes Scheme proposal.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many Members have expressed grave concerns about it, and I would like to start my speech by highlighting one.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If somebody has not been actively putting aside the sum throughout the years, several hundred thousand dollars over, let us say 25 years, at a 2% to 4% interest rate is a huge liability on the home sellers and their children at the point, especially if we do not have any additional housing subsidies from the Government, which I have yet to hear PSP mention in the proposal.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yet we also know that many Singaporeans relocate because they have genuine needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: That means that if they sell at that point, the new BTOs under PSP's plan would be more expensive compared to today's BTO because of the many additional grants that HDB provides the home owners, especially those families with lower income.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our public housing is affordable, accessible, inclusive and well-designed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As a GPC Member of Defense and Foreign Affairs, I often host visiting politicians and officials from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our housing and urban planning policies are very well-regarded and many nations seek to replicate them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, policies need to reflect changing aspirations, a core issue that many people have today is centred around the affordability of mature estates' new BTOs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I understand Singaporeans' concerns when they see the prices where they are.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But yet, those who have gotten flats in attractive locations gain significantly more housing equity after the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This upside needs to be considered when we are talking about affordability, especially of new BTOs in mature estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am not saying that we should abandon efforts to make housing more affordable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Extra grants can certainly help first-time home owners, but reducing prices means that the Government must cut back in other areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, we must ask ourselves, what are we willing to sacrifice?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Instead of only lowering BTO prices, can we look at the issue at a different vantage point?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we lower our peoples' expenses by helping them acquire BTOs close to their family members living in mature estates?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Those who do not get the place in this group can still join the general ballot; three, HDB can build more 3G flats in mature states; and finally, HDB can reduce speculative demand on BTOs in mature estates or attractive locations by introducing some of the criteria from our new PLH scheme. let me delve into the affordability of our public housing in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I recognise that the Government has introduced a number of cooling measures specifically targeting the HDB resale market.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Although the number of flats purchased by PRs is relatively small, I understand, it serves as a sign to our citizens that our Government is using all reasonable measures to cool the market in this exceptional time, prioritising Singaporeans to acquire flats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I would also like to caution MND on adopting PSP's proposal to radically reduce the price of new BTOs by completely disregarding land price in pricing if the flats never sold.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Let us walk through what will happen systematically.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At first look, it seems attractive except that many Singaporeans change of flats and locations as the aspirations in life circumstances change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I mean, we know plenty of Singaporeans relocate to be closer to their jobs, parents or because of the change of marital status.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When they move under PSP's proposal, because they must pay land costs and interests, they will be worse off than today because of the generous grant provided.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is also a question of who will buy the resale flats if the price differential between a new flat without the land cost and the resale flat with the land cost is so big.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Let us not forget that our housing equity forms the largest asset to most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do not even need to wait for the first tranche or MOP to be completed under PSP's proposal to fuel the dire consequences.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At a time when we are still dealing with delayed BTOs due to COVID-19, this flood of new demand will make delays much, much worse.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A collapsing resale market will have significant effects on the retirement adequacy of seniors living in our flats who rely on their housing equity to finance it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is simply unjust to engineer such a dramatic drop in prices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Seniors have no more time to save up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is also a considerable impact to younger Singaporeans who recently bought condominiums.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It will affect SMEs and micro SME owners whose many bank loans for their businesses are secured by their housing equity through personal guarantees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We should stay clear of artificially creating a hard landing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yesterday, in the Chamber, hon Member Cheng Hsing Yao made a wise point.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The value of our land reflects decades of investment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I would also like to humbly add that the value of every square foot of Singapore is also anchored on our sound governance and stable policy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means we pursue stable, reasonable policies that evolve over time and not undertake abrupt, radical shifts to catch prevailing prodigal winds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means we use targeted measures and avoid unnecessary systematic risks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means we add, not deplete our reserves for the tougher journey ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When we opt for savvy slogans over practical policies that benefit Singapore, trust in our system of governance will vanish.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If trust vanishes, so will the value of our land no matter how many miles of fibre optics or MRT lines are buried underneath.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our housing policies are broadly effective, feasible and equitable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Let us build on them and make them better.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Motion put forth by Minister Desmond Lee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Louis Chua Kheng Wee has spoken about the inadequacy of Build-To-Order HDB launches.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Jamus Lim has spoken about the tension between housing as an asset and retirement solution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament Leon Perera has proposed building ahead of demand and the prospect of 70-year leases to build up CPF retirement funds and Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament Gerald Giam has spoken of how to arrest resale prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for my speech, it is in four parts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will touch on how housing policy has evolved in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will discuss where we stand on both affordability and accessibility of HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, I will make some inquiries on how land is priced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And finally, I will ask the Minister some questions on public housing and taxpayer subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was intended that through home ownership, Singaporeans would have a tangible stake in Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The policy then was that flats would only be sold to families earning less than $800 a month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Home Ownership for the People Scheme did not really take off at the beginning as not many people could afford the 20% downpayment in cash to secure a flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This changed dramatically some four years later in 1968 when CPF funds were made available to pay for public housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This allowed the Government to purchase a great deal of land at low prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This historical fact accounts for the ever so often heard view that because HDB bought the land cheaply and since that land would be returned to the state after 99 years, there is scope or there could be scope for the state to take a different, more enlightened view about land costs in order to make public housing more affordable and consider other approaches beyond strict market pricing to keep HDB flats affordable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, property prices in Singapore kept rising.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Lease decay did not factor heavily in the public consciousness as many flats were relatively new.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, a serious correction to housing prices hit hard on the back of the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After the 2001 elections, then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong promised a review of costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Much was expected of the Economic Review Committee, in particular, the Land Working Group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then, land costs came into the gun sights of those worrying about the cost of doing business in Singapore and the cost of housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Instead of precipitating bold changes, the Land Working Group took the view that it was tough to demolish and rebuild Singapore's land policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The group's report restated the constraints policy-makers faced while advocating a greater role to be played by the private sector in the provision of public housing and even suggesting the extension of grants for private home buyers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a country, we have been at the current property cycle before – more recently, slightly more than a decade ago, when the prices of HDB flats increased rapidly after the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, much less was broadcasted about the fact that the increased subsidies to make flats affordable would be paid by taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is significant because a large part of the government solution whenever HDB prices went, perhaps, out of hand, would be to resort to deploying more taxpayer monies, ostensibly in greater quanta, to make up the difference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A significant overlay to the property cycles over the last few decades has been the public expectation that HDB flats would be ever appreciating assets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This incorrect expectation was created, perpetuated and not corrected by previous PAP Governments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A more responsible narrative would have informed the public that capital gains will be possible only in the short to medium term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It should have been made clear to all that quite simply, public housing on a 99-year lease cannot be expected to appreciate endlessly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few years ago, then Minister for National Development Lawrence Wong finally spoke the unvarnished truth about 99-year leases – that flats would be returned to HDB and only a small percentage of flats would undergo the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was a highly negative public reaction to this clarification.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One academic at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy put it this way, "The government hasn't been entirely consistent in their messaging with regard to housing policy, which created the uncertainty and anxiety." Singaporeans, or at least some Singaporeans, felt that there was a reneging of what they perceived as an asset appreciation promised by PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to the second part of my speech – where are we now?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Property prices in Singapore have soared in the last couple of years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As far as HDB flats are concerned, resale prices are breaking new records.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In most parts of the developed world, property prices are moderating or falling because of rising interest rates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since the US Federal Reserve System started raising rates in March 2022, the situation in other countries has developed in a normal way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When interest rates rise, property transactions decrease and prices drop.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, despite steeply rising interest rates for nearly a year now, prices have shot sky high.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is only because of new cooling measures that the property market shows signs of moderating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact of Singapore's property prices going in a different direction from many other countries provides some proof that external circumstances are not the cause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As far as property in Singapore is concerned, the Singapore Government controls the supply of new property in the market, both in the public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Government also controls the number of new citizens and permanent residents (PRs) and has full information on birth rates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It controls the inflow of work and employment pass holders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government knows the application rates for HDB flats and controls HDB allocation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government is the largest landowner and developer of land and is the regulator of land policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because of a preponderance of control over land supply, the Government is in the best position to ensure housing prices remain affordable and stable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The levers at the disposal of the Government do not just include introducing cooling measures overnight by way of fiat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They include building public housing ahead of demand and stepping up private land sales to meet demand at reasonable prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact is that the prices of HDB BTO flats, resale flats and private condominiums generally move in synchrony – which brings me to today's two Motions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The different phrasing of today's two Motions indicates the different thrust of each.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government's Motion implies that HDB flats have been kept affordable and accessible while PSP's Motion suggests that flats are now not affordable and accessible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some of the difference could be due to a different understanding of what each word means and represents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would argue that affordable HDB flats mean HDB flat pricing that is not out of synchrony with salaries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the rise in resale flat prices, should not be perceived to outstrip salary increases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Million-dollar HDB flats no longer make the news.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such sales take place even in areas such as Woodlands, heightening the anxieties of parents and young families and adults with regard to affordability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In all likelihood, either these subsidies will grow ever larger to keep HDB flats affordable or more subsidies will have to be recouped at the point of sale, similar to how it is proposed for Prime Location Public Housing (PLH) flats currently.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would be a somewhat analogous albeit different situation to the PSP's proposal for deferred land cost by way of its Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In one situation, in this case, PLH flats, a designated portion of taxpayer subsidies are returned to the Consolidated Fund.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the other, land cost will be returned into the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government regularly trots out that the HDB housing backlog after the Asian Financial Crisis as a reason for not wanting to build excessively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this sacred cow is one that needs to be slaughtered, particularly because of the serious implications an overheated housing market has on public housing prices for the common man and woman.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, the orthodoxy is one that feeds itself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Government does not release adequate parcels of land quickly enough, a bubble can rapidly form, one that has a direct implication on HDB BTO and resale prices and the prospect of an increase in taxes to fund subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Accessibility includes not just being able to apply for and book a flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also means securing a flat in a timely way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When people get their flats later, they may also put off having children earlier, a largely perverse policy outcome in the face of our efforts to encourage young couples to form families and have children.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The decision to build to order rather than ahead of demand has likely had an impact on the reproductive rates of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It should not come as a surprise if couples and newer generations of Singaporeans want to occupy their own home before starting a family and having children.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This will address accessibility in a meaningful way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The multi page advertisement from HDB in The Straits Times is dated 3 July 1989.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is titled, "The new HDB booking system, how it works for you." And I quote from this newspaper article: "Under the booking system, HDB will announce every quarter, the building contracts it has awarded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The number of units of each type of flat, their location, layout and design and the price range for each type of flat in each location as well as the expected date of completion will also be made known.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: HDB will simultaneously release broad plans of the building contracts for the subsequent nine months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The number and type of flat and their locations will also be made known.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The details provided in these broad plans may change depending on the demand for flats in the area.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thus, HDB will in effect announce a rolling 12-month building programme every three months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It will do the same at the start of every quarter and applicant who has booked a flat will normally take possession of his flat in about two and a half years after booking." Today, the BTO system is both similar and different to the booking system of 1989 in some respects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The BTO system today does not promise flats for buyers in two and a half years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, the downside of this pre-BTO model, which ensures an ample supply of flats is that in the event of a "black swan" episode, like the Asian Financial Crisis, there may well be an excess stock of flats which take time to clear, including administrative costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But in that worst-case scenario, new accessibility options can be considered, for example, HDB would be able to offer excess flats towards schemes like the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme, which is, oversubscribed even today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How is it that the HDB could build high-quality flats at a much faster rate decades ago compared to today, even after the introduction of productivity measures, such as prefabrication technology?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister make a commitment to bring accessibility to commitments made in 1989?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government currently sets land costs at fair market value to the price of flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has sought to address that the land cost component of HDB flat prices from a new perspective, through the PSP Affordable Homes Scheme proposal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government would be familiar with the gist of this proposal as it was originally put forward by a researcher from The Institute of Policy Studies, a Government think tank about a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The idea of the land cost for public housing being accounted for differently is not new.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There have been calls from the public and in the mainstream media to see how land cost can be dealt with to make HDB prices more affordable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And these come from a good place, and they should not be received by accusations of wanting to raid the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2002, The Business Times published a reader's letter which said, "land is purchased and assigned to HDB by the Singapore Land Authority.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The actual land costs on the assignment to HDB should not be governed by the market, as the role of HDB must include the important social objective to provide public housing to those who are unable to participate in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a fundamental policy issue which needs to be acknowledged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We need to be more transparent with regard to the cost of land assignment, so that the public can constructively and actively participate in examining the formula of land assignment to HDB." In 2013, on the back of the "Our Singapore Conversation", a Straits Times editorial titled, "Pondering next phase of public housing" stated, "When the HDB's key mission of building affordable homes has to go hand-in-hand with broader considerations, a variety of fresh ideas deserved to be explored.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those floated by National Development Minister Khaw Boon Wan recently are lower-priced BTO flats with a longer Minimum Occupation Period before these can be sold on the open market.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A shorter lease to match cheaper prices and the separation of new flats from others by allowing resale only to the HDB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On this point, I have some questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm if the words, "not much lower cost than its fair market value" – the emphasis being on not much lower – as stated in the POFMA direction, does it suggest that land for HDB flats can be sold to HDB at a price lower than its market value, as established by the Chief Valuer?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, under what circumstances can this be done?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In comparison, such an interpretation would not be inconsistent with the concept of a reserve price for sites sold under the Government Land Sales, GLS, for private housing, and industrial GLS programmes which are pegged to 85% of the estimated market valuation of each site.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Tenderers will qualify if they bid more than 85% of the assessed market value of the land.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If they bid less than up to 85%, the tender exercise can be aborted or is aborted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the 15% discount on the market price of land or the reserve price under GLS programmes constitute a draw on past reserves?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And will the President's approval be required for such land sales which are sold below market valuation, and if not, why not?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on a recent Parliamentary Question by Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament, Mr Louis Chua Kheng Wee, we also know that the Government does not automatically rule out bids below the reserve price for GLS sites.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that the award of a site depends on the prevailing market conditions, number of independent bids received and the specific circumstances of each site.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would such exceptions provide enough reason and context to review how the Government prices land for public housing with a view to gradually cool the market?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Conceptually, this would not be dissimilar to the fiat the Government can wield in not ruling out tender bids below the reserve price for private land.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now come to the final section of my speech with questions for the Minister on taxpayer subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are taxpayers' subsidies and they represent the "loss" that the HDB incurs on the HDB's home ownership programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This loss is fully funded and made good by the taxpayer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his oral reply to my supplementary question last month, Minister said that resale prices had increased to around 28% or 29% over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But that BTO prices had been kept stable, ostensibly because taxpayer subsidies made up the difference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It must follow that Government expenditure would be reallocated or directed from some other programmes to fund the homeownership programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This fact alone, one that has significant fiscal implications – but also a fact the Government, to my knowledge has thus far, never canvass as a reason to raise taxes would make it important for the Government to provide a breakdown of the dollar value of taxpayer subsidies for the home ownership programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The broad answer given to my Parliamentary Question on a breakdown of taxpayer subsidies filed last month was that the taxpayer subsidies are not the same across BTO developments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This reply raises important, questions of fairness and equity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mature BTO flats are more highly sought after compared to non-mature flats precisely because there is a greater profit and upside to be made after the Minimum Occupation Period, bringing the question of subsidies into acute focus.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on the Minister's reply, it would appear that an applicant who succeeds in securing a BTO flat in a mature estate where flats can be significantly more expensive, benefits from more taxpayer subsidies than one who secures a flat in a non-mature estate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With respect to these taxpayer subsidies, a distinction between mature and non-mature BTO flats is important because any deployment and subsequent recovery of subsidies for the home ownership programme ought to be, in principle, equitable and progressive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, different subsidies allocated for different HDB BTO developments did not prevent the former Minister for National Development Khaw Boon Wan from sharing the dollar value of subsidies for specific BTO developments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On 9 September 2012, in a written answer to a question by Member of Parliament Ellen Lee, even without being specifically asked, the Minister shared the example of Waterway Banks – a BTO project launched in November 2011 in Punggol.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The then Minister shared that this project had 1,016 units of 2- to 4-room flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The then Minister's answer starkly makes the point that there is actually no reason that can adequately explain why the current Government does not release the information on the taxpayer subsidies allocated for each BTO development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Compounding the matter of limited transparency on subsidies further, is the application of the resale levy at the point of sale.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The policy intent of the resale levy is to reduce the taxpayer subsidy the buyer receives on their second subsidised HDB BTO flat and ensures a fairer distribution of subsidies between first and second timers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the point of sale of their first subsidised flat, the first time buyers of both a mature and non-mature BTO flat must return some portion of the taxpayers' subsidies they originally received through the resale levy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Until the Minister releases more information, it is open to question if the payment of the resale levy, which crucially does not distinguish between mature and non-mature flats, is either fair or equitable in view of the potentially wide variation between the original subsidies allocated to either lessee upon the purchase of their first BTO flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope this information is forthcoming so alternative pricing models for HDB flats, a fair allocation of taxpayer subsidies and new policy proposals can be considered and advanced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The single amendment is as follows: in line three, to delete "endorses the commitment of the Government to" and insert "calls on the Government to intensify its efforts to meet".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of the amendment?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Singh, do you have copies made for amendments?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The proposed amendment by the Leader of the Opposition to the Motion on Affordable and Accessible Public Housing is in order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I ask Members to consider whether the current anxieties of Singaporeans do not warrant greater effort by the PAP Government to review its commitment to affordability and accessibility with respect to public housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It would also mean that young couples and first-time Singaporean families who cannot secure a HDB BTO flat in a timely fashion and are pushed to the resale market where resale prices are higher than they have ever been – are not seeking better outcomes from public housing policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We know from our engagement with Singaporeans that this is not the case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the circumstances, it would be thoroughly underwhelming and missing the point for this House to carry a Motion which endorses the commitment of the Government's effort on affordability and accessibility thus far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For the record, the Workers' Party has no fundamental objection to the PSP's Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: One PAP Member inferred the PSP's Motion to be insidious.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Workers' Party does not share that view.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We do not read any implication into it but see it as a call on the Government to review its public housing policies with the view towards greater affordability and accessibility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is something the Government, to its credit, does regularly in response to feedback.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For example, at the last Committee of Supply debates, specifically on HDB Priority Schemes, the Workers' Party called on the Government to increase the ballot opportunities for first-timer, married couples with children to secure flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Sometime later, the Government announced changes broadly along these lines.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is, that the words proposed to be left out, be left out.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The House has resolved on 6 February 2023 that the Motions on Affordable and Accessible Public Housing, and Public Housing Policies and on any other amendments moved by Members on these two motions be proceeded simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In accordance with the decision of this House to have a simultaneous debate on both Motions and amendments, we will proceed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any clarifications for the Leader of the Opposition before I call on Minister Desmond Lee?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just a short point of order which probably does not require a reply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But it would have been helpful if the Leader of the Opposition had put forward the amendment earlier so that Members would have had the benefit of seeing the amendment and have been able to debate it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not, of course, that it comes just after everyone else has spoken and just before the Minister will speak.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I just wanted to respond to say that it reminded me very much of the Justice Motion that I tabled in November of 2020 when Mr Murali put forward an amendment to the Motion at the last minute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, indeed, I am sure Mr Murali had good reason to do so because I think his amendment came after listening to various speeches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this amendment, I think, could have been done a lot earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But it is all right, we will deal with it as it comes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I now call the Minister for National Development to make his reply on his Motion on Affordable and Accessible Public Housing, followed by Mr Leong Mun Wai for his reply on his Motion on Public Housing Policies thereafter.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will put the question in respect of each Motion to the House for voting.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, I would like to thank Members on both sides of this House who have shared your views on public housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is an important topic for this House.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is an important topic for Singapore and this discussion is taking place at the time that we are in, after the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Residents look for their own housing on the open market, do their sums, borrow if they have to and find their way – whether to buy, rent or some other arrangement.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Governments intervene largely by enabling private developers to build and sell homes to people.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They may provide public housing but this is usually as a social safety net for the lower income.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In Singapore, we have taken a very unique approach, one that has been developed over the decades since Independence and continually improved to achieve two very important fundamental objectives.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are building homes to give Singaporeans a roof over their heads, but we are also building diverse communities for Singaporeans to live, bond and experience life together.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In doing so, we build a nation as one people.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, we want to give Singaporeans a stake in the nation by having a home they call their own and sharing in the progress by unlocking the value of their homes and growing their nest egg.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To achieve this, we harness a combination of national policy and Government resources on the one side and elements of the open market on the other side, to help unlock the value of people’s homes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But in so doing, we must be very clear-eyed about long-term sustainability, as many Members who spoke during the debate have underscored.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To prevent the resale market from running ahead of economic fundamentals, we implemented two rounds of cooling measures and are seeing some moderation in the rate of increase in resale prices.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are still closely monitoring the housing market and we hope that Members can be patient and watch as it develops.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I have also committed to Singaporeans that we will not stand by but will continue to enhance the accessibility and affordability of public housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We acknowledge the concerns of first-timer couples trying to set up their very first home and have been studying ways to better help them get their first homes faster.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We understand the concerns that people have raised about higher BTO prices in mature estates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have sought to address some of these concerns through the Prime Location Public Housing (PLH) Model in the more central and very attractive locations in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will continue to review our housing models to ensure affordability and accessibility of flats in other mature estates and choice locations, while avoiding an excessive windfall gain to those who successfully book a flat in such areas.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, the Leader of Opposition spoke about Central Weave @ AMK.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The price he cited was that of the most expensive 5-room flat on the top floor in a location in the heart of Ang Mo Kio Central, next to a hawker centre, next to a wet market, next to two shopping malls, next to the MRT station, next to the bus interchange, next to parks and other amenities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It was a conscious decision to build public housing, as opposed to private housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Recently, there were GLS sites and launches of private housing in Ang Mo Kio, not in Ang Mo Kio Central.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The prices for private housing, which I think you can compare and are clear for all to see, is that there is a clear distinction in prices between the HDB flats in this project in Ang Mo Kio Central and private housing launched by the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the brochure itself, members of the public as well as Members of this House can see the range of BTO prices before grants as well as the market comparables for HDB resale prices nearby, which after adjustments, will give you a broad sense of the gap between what is available on the resale market and what is available as subsidised housing in a choice mature estate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But what I have also emphasised is that this Government needs to provide affordable and accessible public housing, not just for this generation but also for future generations of Singaporean.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are a small city-state, 720 square kilometres with many competing needs and our scarce land needs to be carefully stewarded.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will create space to meet the needs of today's Singaporeans and tomorrow's generation, but this will involve rejuvenating and recycling land, and building more intensively.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Singapore has no natural resources to rely on.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have to create and build up the fiscal resources needed to support the home ownership aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our housing policies also reflect our values of prudence and sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must not subsidise housing at the expense of other equally important needs for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must not enhance housing accessibility and affordability of this generation, by robbing our future generations, whether of land or fiscal resources, or the reserves which are intended to put them in better state, through thick or thin.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is what a responsible Government should do.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Above all, we must continue to build a nation of home owners, for this generation and the next, to continue the legacy our forefathers have started.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We firmly believe in home ownership, as it provides us the stability to build our families and raise our children, give us a sense of rootedness in Singapore and allow us to have a stake in our country's progress.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Home ownership has worked for us and we need to continue with the good work to make it work for the next generation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is why we sell HDB flats on 99-year leasehold, which strikes a balance between providing a home-for-life, asset appreciation and enabling us to rejuvenate our city and build new homes for the next generation too.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Hazel Poa, the Leader of the Opposition and Mr Louis Chua asked why we did not build even more and even faster.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, several Members have sounded a word of caution, taking a longer-term view and looking at the lessons of the past.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I have just said that we are already doing that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, we are already overseeing almost 100 BTO projects island-wide, at different stages of construction.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: By contract value, HDB is not just the largest housing developer, but also exceeds all the other private residential housing contracts combined by more than 50%.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we are already building aggressively and at large scale.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We should also remember that HDB is not the only one ramping up, especially after the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Since the pandemic started to subside, the overall pace of building and construction on our island has gone up very significantly.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Individuals, businesses, private developers, organisations, Government agencies are all pushing ahead with their important projects while doing catch-up on COVID-19-related delays suffered by existing projects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Fiscal resources, foreign manpower and construction capacity are not without their limits.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Several Members, including Ms Hazel Poa, Mr Louis Chua and the Leader of the Opposition, have suggested that the Government has under-estimated demand and under-built the supply of flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Hazel Poa suggested that the Government knows the number of marriages and the immigration numbers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Leader of Opposition has indicated a wider range of parameters.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We do in fact have models that take into account many considerations – marriages, births, deaths, income levels, economic conditions and cycles, demand for different housing types and so on – in trying to project the real demand for flats and for property in general.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, as we all know, it is not a perfect science and it certainly cannot account for sudden shocks and what sudden shocks can cause in terms of human psychology and market behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, for many years before COVID-19 hit, application rates for BTO flats were low and in fact, the resale market was soft.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I had mentioned all of these in my opening speech.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I trust Members, including Members of the Opposition, had listened to that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, my colleague, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann, had emphasised those points.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Then COVID-19 hit, the dynamics shifted rapidly and we are in the current situation where demand for housing shot up.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The housing market is highly sentiment-driven and demand can suddenly appear, or disappear.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the height of the property boom in the mid-1990s, there were as many as 150,000 buyers in the queue for public housing and the wait for a flat could be as long as seven years.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, when the Asian Financial Crisis struck in 1997, the queue vanished, virtually overnight, some say.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because of the unintended oversupply, home buyers could walk in to buy ready flats in the early 2000s.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, home owners paid a heavy price, with flat prices, or resale flat values, staying depressed.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some who bought flats just before the crisis ended up with negative equity and even lost their homes and hard-earned savings.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The many unsold flats represented a waste of taxpayers' money.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The holding cost incurred from the vacant housing stock is not inconsequential.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It was money that could have been spent on other uses – healthcare, education and other areas, especially after a financial crisis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: People who were sitting in this House at the time were asking lots of questions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I can tell you that if you were to look at the records, the mood was quite the opposite of what you are hearing today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Several Members of Parliament like Miss Cheryl Chan and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin also pointed out that the danger of oversupply is real.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Should there be a persistent or significant oversupply of housing, this imposes a downward pressure on the housing market, which in turn hurts the asset values of all flat owners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even the Workers' Party is cognisant of the implications of an oversupply, as seen in their 2019 Working Paper on HDB resale prices.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But today, with perfect hindsight, they are asking about actions of the years before.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The paper mentioned, "Assuming an average household size of 3.3, this would mean that around 9,000 or so new dwelling units are required annually.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Completions within the same time period have far exceeded the resident population growth.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Private vacancies have only started to inch down, but there are still around 12,000 private units completing up to 2022." And then it goes on to say, "Will the HDB have a vacancy rate problem, compounded by a still steady stream of 16,000 to 17,000 BTO units in the last few years, which will continue to increase supply up to 2022?" This was a report commissioned within the Workers' Party, quoting experts from the property sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 2019, they cautioned HDB from persisting in building 16,000 to 17,000 BTO units, instead saying: would vacancies cause problems?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Better just go down to around 9,000 BTO units or so because they made a lot of assumptions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They marshalled a lot of data and experience, and this was the recommendation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, in 2019, the Workers' Party was recommending that HDB should only build 9,000 dwelling units or so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Had we tapered down our supply to the Workers' Party's levels in 2019, or listened to you and your experts, I think our BTO shortage would be even greater today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, I think we all accept that the best of models cannot, firstly, fully account for black swan events.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This shows just how difficult it is to accurately predict residential property demand, or for that matter, the direction and size of movements in the property market.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We therefore need to be careful in calibrating flat supply to meet demand.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Most importantly, it is important for us not to try to ascribe a wrong set of reading of the facts because before COVID-19 struck, the data, in terms of application rates across the board, as well as resale prices, indicated that the housing market was relatively stable – until around the time of COVID-19 when the situation changed.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: During the Asian Financial Crisis, demand vanished and prices plunged.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: COVID-19 is a crisis of a different sort, but it is still a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, with perfect hindsight, we still make conjectures as to what we think caused this change in movement.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I described, or attempted to describe, just some of those broad strokes in my opening speech.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, I think it is very important for us to recognise what we ourselves had said in 2019 as we sit here and try to pontificate about what the Government had or had not done.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Several Members, Mr Leong Mun Wai and Mr Jamus Lim for instance, have also put forward proposals that effectively will result in a draw on past reserves.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Most of the points have been dealt with by my colleague, Minister Indranee Rajah, but in fact, Mr Jamus Lim sought to justify that paying lower land price is a way of "being present" for the current generation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Leong proposed the Affordable Homes Scheme, which as my colleague, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann and many Members of this House have explained, is not a better alternative to addressing the challenges of affordability and accessibility, compared to what we have today and compared to what we intend to do and are studying to do.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Minister Indranee Rajah has also explained that if the occupiers of flats under this scheme do not sell the flats, then by leaving land costs out of the equation of this proposal, it is effectively a draw on the reserves.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have also heard many suggestions on improving public housing affordability.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have shared that we price new BTO flats based on affordability, not at the median level as the Workers' Party has repeatedly called for, or what was originally in the PSP's manifesto of 2020 – though, having heard Mr Leong, I am not sure if the manifesto still stands.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have shared that we price new BTO flats based on affordability for different income levels.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Based on the market value of the comparable flats, we then apply a significant discount to ensure they remain affordable to first-time buyers across different income levels, not just at the median.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: On top of that, we provide additional grants for first-timer families, with more grants to those who need them the most.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: What it means is not just a statistical fact.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Nine in 10 of these families use less than a quarter of their total household income to pay for their mortgage instalments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They can finance their HDB loan completely with CPF, with little to no cash needed.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The MSR figures are even lower for those at lower-income percentiles with the higher grants they receive.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In other words, they can service their mortgages entirely from their monthly CPF contributions, with no cash outlay.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is an appropriate time in which I deal with the Leader of the Opposition's questions repeatedly about transparency and the extent of the subsidies given to buyers in the mature estates and the non-mature estates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I have explained and my colleague Ms Indranee Rajah has tried to explain.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, in this speech, just moments earlier, and in my opening speech, I tried to explain and break down how we price HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Also, in reply to Mr Gerald Giam in a Parliamentary Question, I thought I tried to explain very clearly and answer some of his questions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When we build HDB flats, we look at the market comparables for HDB because it is public housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: HDB is already the most transparent on its pricing and costs than any other property developer.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: You asked for more information but the information is already there and explained at length to the Member.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Look at the information when we put out at every launch.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For every project, we have the range of BTO prices, which are subsidised, and right next to it is a column of the comparable resale prices.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have to make some adjustments because depending on the level, depending on the amenities, depending on the tenure, we have to make adjustments and these are adjustments made using valuation principles.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, once you have done that, you can see that this difference in the brochures, in the information that we put out, for every launch, for many, many years already, broadly reflects the extent of the market discount, which is real and which buyers can realise after MOP when they sell because the BTO price is significantly below market.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But I have also taken pains to explain to the Member that we have to make adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have to recognise that for each flat type, there are different floors and so we put the range.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Likewise, the comparables also have different flat heights.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we put the range to be transparent.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That difference broadly reflects the extent of the market subsidy for the projects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And you can see today that it has become very large compared to, say, 10 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That – and I did not mention in my opening speech – in turn feeds the psychology when you see the resale prices going up and BTO prices remaining almost the same.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There is the sense that BTO is a better deal now, better go for it, especially in good locations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But as I also explained to the Member, if you want to know the extent of the subsidies for each project, you also have to take into account the other half of the picture.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because apart from significant market discounts, you would be familiar with the grants that we give – Proximity Housing Grant, Enhanced CPF Housing Grant, so on and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That has got various parameters, so it is not so straightforward.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It depends on means testing, it depends on flat type, it depends on whether you tap on the scheme for Proximity Housing Grant to open up that grant to yourself.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That gives you a sense of the picture.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that is why Mr Leong Mun Wai's proposal is far more expensive to the ordinary citizen than it is under our scheme and Members who have spoken understand what this is so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The land and construction costs every year is more for our HDB projects than the proceeds we collect because of the discounts we give in terms of market subsidy as well as the grants that are means tested or based on flat type, based on proximity, based on Fresh Start, based on this and that, and the proceeds we collect are significantly less than how much we spend.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Leader of the Opposition makes a good point about whether there is equity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Are we giving people in certain projects more discounts or subsidies than others?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Whether there are more discounts and subsidies, again, depend on those factors, but the broad market discount across all projects, barring PLH, in the same launch is broadly in the same parameter to ensure there is equity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But later on, when they sell, it depends on the resale market, it depends on the condition of the flat.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Property valuers will tell you that, property agents will tell you that, your residents who buy and sell instinctively know that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Okay, maybe we can clarify over coffee later if you need more information.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, that is the extent of the difference.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: You can see that information on the brochures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is the third time I have said that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In terms of HDB as a transparent developer, I have said that it is more transparent on pricing than others.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Construction costs, if you care to know, most private developers will not tell you that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is all a part and parcel of their financial statements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But construction costs are published on HDB's website and GeBIZ, and the cost of building flats and the revenue from sale of flats can be found in HDB's financial statements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: All of these are subject to the Auditor-General's overall supervision.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is more than what private developers typically disclose.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We understand private developers, as I said in my opening speech, do things differently which is probably more intuitively to most of you.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They look at the cost of development, cost of marketing, and recover that cost and price for profit and return.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Deficits are a function of achieving those goals of affordability and accessibility.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As a result of what I have just described, the PSP's proposal is going to be far more expensive to those whom in the ordinary nature of things, buy because they want to have a home and then at some point in time, they need to sell.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Most people do not go into the housing market either thinking this is a home for the rest of my life or going in as a pure speculator.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think it is perfectly human to say, when I buy a home, it is a home.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I am going to spend money, I am going to invest in it.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It may make money, it may lose money, it may break even.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is a lot of effort to move in, renovate and move in and there is social capital to invest in your neighbours and all that, with children in the schools nearby.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But it is not wrong for some of these people to say at some point in time, my life circumstances have changed and I need to sell – not sell to make money but sell because it is part of life's circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, I think if PSP ascribes to everyone who is a reseller that you must then punish them with a certain way of pricing on resale, then I do not think that is being fair to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is not being fair to our own human nature when we are buying homes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yes, there are speculators, but I think most Singaporeans look for a home but hope that also helps with their retirement adequacy, gives them a sense that their asset will appreciate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yes, there will be ups and downs based on the market cycle.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But I think it is not incongruent to expect both, especially if this is the single largest expense or investment of your life.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, therefore, we clearly charge below construction costs and land costs whereas the PSP's proposal is, well, you live here forever.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is an expense, it is a user fee.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many Members have already explained why they think Mr Leong Mun Wai's Affordable Homes Scheme will not work and will not solve the issues we are facing today or tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Gerald Giam reiterated the Workers' Party's proposal to peg non-mature estate home prices at three times the median annual household income.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also very eloquently explained that the fact that people are prepared to spend and invest in a property as opposed to renting because they cannot afford – all these are indicators that give you a sense that BTOs are broadly affordable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, if the Workers' Party says they will want to make significant changes to the Motion because they think that a lot more work needs to be done for affordability, then I think they have not explained how in bringing the HPI from the current level to three; and in fact, for some, it is already below three and you are going to raise it to meet your HPI of three artificially, by increasing prices for the lower income to meet your dogmatic three, I think an important question is how will you fund it?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
