text: Will you fund it by, like how Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has said, valuing housing so much like a social good, like a park, like a hospital, like a school, or like roads – $1 a metre he said.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, while the proposal sounds attractive, it ignores the trade-off that far lower prices would attract even more flat applicants, whether they genuinely need housing or not.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It also does not address the windfall gains enjoyed by flat buyers, some of whom may be from the higher income levels and, quite apart from first-time BTO sale, how do you ensure the affordability of the resale market over time.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Not us, but our forefathers have set the right example.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They demonstrated the ethos of hard work, prudence, selflessness and sacrifice.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They not only resettled in and housed a generation – and it was by no means an easy feat – but also built up the resources that we enjoy today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must embrace the same values and not pursue housing policies that benefit ourselves at the expense of future generations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My colleague Minister of States Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim has already explained how we proactively planned ahead and made provisions to help seniors monetise their flats to supplement their retirement.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, I was speaking about the new housing models that cater to seniors – and we are not done yet.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We continue to make an extra effort to help the lower income own their own homes, so that their next generation will have a leg-up in life, which another social element behind public housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To ensure that we help lower-income groups fulfil their home ownership aspirations, our housing grants are tiered such that they receive more in grants.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have also introduced the ComLink Rental Scheme, enhanced the Fresh Start Housing Scheme and set up the Home Ownership Support Team to closely support rental families towards progress, stability and the path to home ownership.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And I was cheered when I heard Ms Janet Ang speak earlier about actual families that she works with.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I have talked about the past, a few years before COVID-19, to show how we have kept building and keeping pace with housing demand and needs, how we try to build a model to anticipate, how during the COVID-19 black swan event, things turned out the way they are, what we are doing, the commitment that we have made to address these issues openly, assiduously, transparently, and my colleagues at MND and HDB and many other agencies are working really hard to tackle today's challenges.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But we also must look at affordability and accessibility and the public housing of Singapore into the future as well.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, the important question is, will we have enough land and resources to build new and better homes for younger Singaporeans, and the generation after them and the generation after that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And we will be able to find the space to build homes for Singaporeans for the long term.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There are a number of ways we do this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And these are some of the exciting new bounds in our ambition as a distinctive city and enduring home.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, we will continually redevelop older parts of our city and in due course, also rejuvenate our older estates through the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme, or VERS.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This provides us the opportunity to redevelop towns in a sustainable manner and ensure equitable housing through the generations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But will we, the people of Singapore today and tomorrow continue to afford public housing?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, we build and price BTOs to ensure affordability for Singaporeans of various income levels.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Access to BTOs is based on income eligibility and other criteria.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This allows us to ensure BTO flats can continue to remain affordable over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But they come with additional conditions to ensure equity and fairness, so that we ensure a good mix of Singaporeans from more diverse walks of life, while ensuring fairness between PLH owners and other flat owners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For choice projects in the mature estates, we must study carefully how to continue to keep BTO prices there affordable, and Members have given many useful suggestions in this regard.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For the resale market, we can also continue to ensure that it grows as an asset for a good part of its duration, for the good part of a buyer’s life and yet remain affordable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: More importantly, we do this by growing the economy and growing the incomes of Singaporeans at every level.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, their incomes grow, and their ability to spend, their ability to invest, their ability to look after their families grow.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And by no means are we saying through this Motion that all is well and good and that nothing needs fixing, and it is a perfect system.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As I said in the opening speech and as reported in the papers, our system is far from perfect but it has achieved through the generations, the outcomes that we have laid on the table today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And there are things that we have to tackle today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There are the imbalances of COVID-19 but there are also work-in-progress pieces as part of social policy to ensure affordability and accessibility as our households change, our society matures, our economy evolves and expectations change.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that is our commitment to those twin goals.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Public housing has been and remains accessible and affordable broadly to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And in the next lap, we will face new challenges in terms of ageing infrastructure, more binding land constraints, climate change and we will need our resources, our reserves and our wherewithal to go through them.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As I set out in my opening speech, we disagree with the PSP’s claims in its Motion and decided to table our own Motion.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Throughout this debate, Members from both sides of the House also agree that fiscal sustainability is imperative.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, Mr Leong and the PSP’s position seems also to have shifted, from pricing flats based on median incomes in the 2020 manifesto; to December 2022 where they proposed eliminating land cost totally from the cost of developing public housing; to today, a deferred payment scheme where owners pay the full cost of land with accrued interest only when they want to sell the flat, as we learnt yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think Mr Leong and many Members may disagree whether it is a mischaracterisation or whether it is military strategy, I think it is quite clear to most of us, including objective observers, that there has been a change.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I welcome the convergence of both sides of the House on this principle of sustainability, which lies at the heart of our Motion.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I was quite taken by what Mr Cheng Hsing Yao said, and I would like to quote briefly from him.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He spoke sensibly and passionately about policy trade-offs yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He said: “An enlightened public leader will carefully weigh the pros and cons of each policy option, never downplay the trade-offs, never sacrifice the long-term benefits for short-term gratification.” He also cautioned all of us in this House that if we were to give in to the “appealing rhetoric that understates the trade-offs and real costs", “eventually, it is still the people and the man in the street that suffer the most”.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is not a perfect system, there are things we need to improve today and tomorrow, but to say it is fundamentally through and through unaffordable and inaccessible and needs a radical change of the kind that he is proposing together with his party, is something we cannot accept.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And if I may say, I believe the Workers' Party also agrees with the Affordable Homes Scheme as part of supporting the Motion, but you can clarify.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And as we said, we think the proposals put forward by the PSP do not address today's problems and certainly do not address tomorrow's problems.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Disruptions from the pandemic have caused imbalances, which we are working hard to address.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As I said earlier, our system is not perfect, but we keep improving it and striving to make it better.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And we have a strategy to ensure public housing remains affordable and accessible into the future.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Stand with us, support our Motion, support the plans for today and tomorrow, and let us work together on our public housing journey.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As for the Workers' Party's proposal, I think the fact that we have a commitment to the twin goals implies this spirit of always wanting to improve, that there are issues that we face today and tomorrow's challenges are something we have to keep an eye on.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think that is evident from the opening speech, that is evident from my colleagues' speeches, that is evident from the speeches of speakers in the House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I just have two quick clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am wondering if the Chief Valuer – and I appreciate that this is an independent office – is provided guidance by the Government that land designated for public housing should embed stronger public considerations; just like how land for other kinds of public priorities may differ from commercial uses?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Would the Government then accept this valuation as acceptable for channelling into reserves and that this would not then constitute a raid on reserves that would require Presidential approval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And if the answer is indeed yes, and I will wait for the response, but what then would be the constraints behind the Government providing such guidance to the Chief Valuer?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Because it surely already provides some form of guidance for different classes of land.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And just for clarification, in my speech, I had mentioned that $1 pricing for land for road but that was actually for the Land Betterment Charge and not in the context of what I am suggesting public housing land be priced that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But he or she will apply the valuation principles that are accepted and value land on the basis of its use.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Public housing land is zoned for public housing and I think the Chief Valuer would be in command of the necessary information to understand what public housing is about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We can share information with him or her, and it is available publicly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But to say that we should – I do not know whether the Member is asking us to – persuade the Chief Valuer to accept his method of valuation as something that is acceptable, I think the profession as a whole would not accept the Member's strategy of valuation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it is always open for Workers' Party to make representations to the relevant departments to advance reasons why the Workers' Party's method of valuation is professionally acceptable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And I also note that Minister has said to Member of Parliament Mr Leong Mun Wai in a Parliamentary Question response that the Government does expect in the near future for housing demand to be robust due to strong household formation and societal trends towards smaller households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, knowing now that effects and circumstances of housing demand has changed and demand will remain robust, I think the question then is do we decide that we need supply or not.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And I think it is also important to point out that the context of this paragraph was really in the context of urban renewal and in the subsequent paragraph, Minister would also see that we clearly stated that the BTO projects should continue, just that it would be supplemented by supply from flats that are acquired under the USB.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On his first point, I hope the Member understands where we are coming from and that we meant well when I said what I said earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We acknowledged that there is a high demand today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is clear from the high BTO application rates across the board, but especially in mature estates and choice locations, that there is high demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is broad-based demand but there is also market psychology at work and COVID-19 had a lot to do with that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We and my colleagues and the construction industry are working very hard to make the land available, to take over land to develop public housing, to do the land preparation, to do the work expeditiously but safely and productively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And it was quite clear from the data that before COVID-19 struck, we were building higher than what Workers' Party had proposed and the application rates were low and the resale prices were soft.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To say both to PSP and the Workers' Party that, "Oh, before COVID-19, you all should have anticipated, you should have done this and done that", I think reeks of applying perfect hindsight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I do not think it is fair to my colleagues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That provides more choice, together with BTO flats that we build more productively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I think 2.5 years or three years before COVID-19, the waiting times were certainly less than the waiting times today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you look at the new projects that we build for Singaporeans, the quality of the buildings, the height of the flats, the amenities that we build, the services that we provide, the design of the buildings, I think you would accept that they are quite a different class of public housing than what you cited in the 1980s and 1990s.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A lot of that accounts for why it does take time despite productivity measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The sites we are building in are complicated sites and some of them are more challenging to build.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some private developers will probably not touch those sites.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have certainly learned a lot from this debate because the rebuttal points have been specific and substantial.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we may differ in our policy ideas and recommendations, all of us in this House share a common objective of keeping public housing affordable and accessible for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also agree with Ms Janet Ang that we are here to unite and not divide but that is provided the Government does not treat every alternative ideas as a source of division.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will now give specific responses to the questions and rebuttals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will demonstrate to Mr Murali Pillai and all of you that what PSP has proposed are feasible aspirations based on pain and choice.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because our policies will benefit most Singaporeans but there will be some slight negative effect on some as well, like those who have committed to high-priced resale flats in anticipation of future profits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is no different from some of the other policy proposals made by PAP Members.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I spent a total of 12 years, first studying and later working in Japan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I have a fairly good understanding of what the overuse of property as an economic management tool had done to that country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the lesson I have learned was opposite to what Mr Sitoh has tried to convey.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The property market cannot rise forever at a fast pace.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the long term, any country's population will eventually peak and decline and there will be fewer buyers than sellers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Continued economic growth will then depend on raising productivity and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the more important property investment and speculation become in an economy, the more likely that economy will become less competitive because property speculation and rent seeking are easier and better alternatives to innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Japan, for example, I have seen how the average Japanese has been bogged down by their mortgages, some of which straddle two generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is from that angle that I got worried when I look at the situation in Singapore today – high property prices but a dearth of innovation and creativity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we need is more innovation and entrepreneurial spirit to continue competing effectively with the rest of the world in the Information Age.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A home is a place for a Singaporean to share comfort and love, not a chain that ties him down with a mortgage that needs to be serviced for the larger part of his life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He should spend his life innovating, creating and fulfilling his potential.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans can become knowledge workers only if they are liberated from the bondage of mortgages and high property prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The only saving grace is that our property market is still rising partly because of population growth through immigration.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not want to be left with no choice, however, except accepting a continuous fast pace of immigration, we will have to seriously consider a reset at this stage when the foreigners, especially the Chinese, are still eager to put their money in our property market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I think this is a brilliant opportunity, while our market is very bullish, for us to reset the policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think, for years, policy-makers and policy analysts have debated – maybe we should change our public housing policies, but we are at such a high price already, how do we do it?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think that has been bothering a lot of people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I think this is a brilliant opportunity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fortunately, unlike Japan, we can use our public housing sector as a buffer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can continue to allow foreigners and well-off Singaporeans to invest in our private property market at higher prices but we must maintain an affordable and accessible public housing market so that our young Singaporeans can have the financial security to be enterprising risk takers and build Singapore into a competitive information economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Government thinks it is doing its best, I think there are substantial reasons to think that there needs to be a reset because the current system is not delivering all the outcomes that we desire.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not change the way we price the HDB flats, the lease decay problem will be a problem of every generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are some of the problems that accompany the current housing policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not think in the debate and even what the Minister said just now have fully addressed them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister had concentrated on doing more of the same, sorting out the current tight demand-supply situation, but what is required is a fundamental change in the thinking of what should be the best public housing policies going forward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I must say again that the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme, we had them in mind right from the beginning.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I did not shift my ideas from taking out of land cost and now add that land cost as a deferred land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what are the advantages of the Affordable Homes Scheme?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we are aiming for is to delink the CPF account from the HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Murali Pillai argued that only the Ordinary Account savings can be used for housing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But how many Singaporeans can meet even the basic retirement sum with just their Special Account savings and without having to sell their flat?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the current system, retirement adequacy will only deteriorate further as CPF contributions are capped and remained the same level for many years while HDB prices continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann shared just now that maybe the retirement situation in terms of the CPF saving balances are better than what we have gathered.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But nevertheless, as BTO prices continue to go up, CPF contributions will continue to be depleted.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One thing I want to highlight is that Senior Minister of State Sim Ann had defined the CPF account now as being one that would cater for both buying the HDB flat and for retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CPF account has been pulled into financing the HDB flat from 1968.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The original definition or the original intention of the CPF account is for retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will clarify on that later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want a situation whereby Singaporeans do not have to depend on resale prices for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Members have pointed out that resale prices go up and down.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This proves my point – that retirement adequacy needs to be delinked from housing prices because resale prices go up and down.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is our current system fair to the elderly Singaporeans who may be forced to retire during a recession but have not enough money in their CPF and may therefore have to sell their flat at a lower price point?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not everyone can control when they retire or when they must monetise their flat for retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a real problem and I hope Members on the other side of the House will consider when they are voting for the two Motions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Application for BTOs in popular areas will increase and upper middle-income Singaporeans may be unhappy but that is the cost we have to pay to reduce social inequality.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Mr Xie Yao Quan and Mr Vikram Nair are concerned that the PSP's proposal will cause a collapse in resale prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, a collapse is actually counterintuitive because in the long term, the supply of resale flats will be reduced as new sellers will not sell their flats unless the price is high enough for them to earn a profit after paying for the deferred land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, there will also be support for the resale market from the backlog of housing demand.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, a large pool of buyers who are ineligible for BTO flats, buyers who want to live in a specific location because they want to live near their parents, Permanent Residents and buyers who want to upgrade to a larger flat form a large pool of demand that will underpin the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most importantly, we must bear in mind that in Singapore, the resale market HDB market is still much lower than the private property market, so there is a demand there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I believe that the Affordable Homes Scheme is also aiming at engineering a soft landing of the current surging resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That will be healthy after recent market exuberance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want a buoyant resale market, not an exuberant one.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, to complement that strategy with a Millennial Apartments Scheme, which can increase the number of housing units in the same prime location housing site by building smaller units for rental.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current BTO system, which feeds on the resale market and vice versa, does not make the overall housing market accessible to young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think we all agree that this is detrimental to our total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current system cannot provide a large enough price difference between BTO flats and resale flats to restrain the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the Affordable Homes Scheme, which is based on the clean concept of taking out the land cost for the owner-occupier, can do this and make the overall housing market more accessible to young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I want to address some of the questions raised by Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Henry Kwek on the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two main areas that they have raised.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One is, will the scheme actually increase the holding cost of the buyers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I call that a breakeven price, meaning the land cost is determined today, you add on the interest payment and what would be the price going forward when the buyer wants to sell the flat in the market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The idea is that, this breakeven price should not be much higher than the current price for the current HDB owners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the normal term of a loan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, I propose an idea, but based on the experience that we have in the public housing market, if it is a good idea, then based on the experience accumulated by HDB, we can decide on how much we want to accrue that interest going forward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second thing is, there is a question about what happens if the flat is given to a beneficiary?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the beneficiary need to pay the accumulated interest on the land cost?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The answer is that the beneficiary can live in the flat as long as they are just an occupier.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When they sell the flat, then the same rules apply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They have to return the land cost with the accrued interest to the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if they cannot sell the flat in the market, then they sell the flat back to HDB, based on a formula which I have explained to Ms Carrie Tan just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is based on the user price, minus the location premium and some depreciation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, we can decide on how much depreciation we want to put into the price later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I have addressed the resale market, I have also addressed some of the questions raised by the Members.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will address the impact, or the perceived impact, on the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the advantages of the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme, their implementation will require the Government to change its mindset regarding accounting for land reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes the land cost should not be charged for owner-occupied HDB flats because it is a public good, with all the social benefits that can be shared by society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our proposals are still fair to future generations, because not all the land cost will be lost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are also giving the present generation a leg-up to do better, which is the best inheritance which we can pass on to our future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, Affordable Homes Scheme will make it fairer for future generations who can enjoy HDB flats at the user price, rather than the higher BTO price in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the most consistent and fair treatment for every Singaporean in each generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether it is a draw on reserves, actually we all know that it depends on the definition of use.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the use is to serve a very useful purpose, then we should not hesitate to redefine the use – if public housing land is state land, we can redefine it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If public housing land is defined as state land, then there is no question about the use of reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Still, this cost can be managed under our budget resources and there is no need to actually use the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked about the fiscal implications of our policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But even if we need to fund the whole sum, we will have more than sufficient fiscal resources required for the implementation of the reset.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We only need the Government to do more for Singaporeans, because we actually have the resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has been saving repeatedly, again and again, in many ways, just to take the resources and put it back into the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, reserve accumulation, that is something that you cannot spend unless the President approves it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the Government said, put 50% of the net investment return into reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You can only use 50%, that 50% becomes the net investment return contribution (NIRC), which goes to the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet again, I do not know whether Members noticed, 80% of our NIRC was never used, maybe except during the COVID-19 years, in the current year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most of the years, NIRC was re-parked into endowment and trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, this is the money, 50% of the net investment returns that is supposed to be used for the budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will assume that it should be used for the current year for the benefit of Singaporeans, but the Minister for Finance put that under endowment and trust funds again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the funds, again, are not used in the current year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we can see that we do not need to use any additional reserves at all, we only need to deploy our current resources where and when they are needed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the above, I hope I have addressed most of the Members' questions, but of course, questions are welcomed afterwards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will conclude today's debate, although the conclusion will take some time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members, do know that you are not obliged to ask clarifications if you do not want to.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The asset enhancement policy, which started in the 1990s, may have reached its limit as the price of any asset cannot rise forever, especially one with a lease decay problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is also counter intuitive to believe that a system that relies on rising HDB prices can actually deliver affordability.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The ecosystem developed to sustain the asset enhancement policy, like the BTO supply and pricing systems, as well as the link between CPF retirement funds and housing prices must be reviewed and changed accordingly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have explained why Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme are the way to achieve a reset of the public housing policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When PSP advocates that the land cost be taken out of the pricing of owner-occupied HDB flats, so that every Singaporean in each generation can have access to affordable housing, we also believe that this is in keeping with the spirit with which our Pioneer Generation sacrificed their land for national development.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: A spirit, which the Government might have forgotten from the 1990s onward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Pioneer Generation have responded to the call for national development and sacrificed much when they gave up their land.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These are not just the big landlords and capitalists, but also ordinary Singaporeans, including farmers who were resettled from rural areas, such as Chua Chu Kang, Lim Chu Kang and Punggol, and indigenous Malay fishermen who were resettled from the Southern Islands.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They surrendered their lands to the Government, in the hope that it will be used to improve the lives of Singaporeans, not for the Government to accumulate reserves for the sake of accumulating, with no clear and transparent definition as to what constitutes "a rainy day", when we can use the reserves for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In the run-up to this debate, some descendants of the Pioneer Generation who had given up their land came to see me and asked me to fight for affordable homes for their children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is it not a great irony that a family that had earlier given up its land for a pittance, thus sacrificing housing for his descendants, is now seeing his descendants pay half a million dollars each for a 90 square metre BTO flat?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Thus, PSP believes that it is the Government's duty to live up to the hopes and expectations of the Pioneer Generation and repay them by ensuring their descendants continue to have affordable homes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In Mandarin):   Dear Fellow Singaporeans, I believe many Singaporeans, like me, still remember how Pioneer Generation Singaporeans were forced to sacrifice their land under the Land Acquisition Act in the 1970s and 1980s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Among them, there were big landlords and capitalists, but also many more ordinary Singaporeans including pig farmers in Punggol, villagers in Charn Mao Hern and Koo Chye Sheng, as well as fishermen in Tuas fishing Village.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Most of our forefathers willingly gave up their land to the People's Action Party (PAP) Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They knew that they sacrificed their land and their way of life for the country's development and the interests of the majority.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They believed that the Government would make good use of their land to provide affordable and quality housing for their children and grandchildren and build a better future for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But today, the public housing policy has imposed a heavy burden on the people of all generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Although the land of the Pioneer Generation was acquired by the Government at a low price, their children and grandchildren could not benefit directly from it as HDB has to buy land at market prices to build HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: While BTO prices are not pegged to market prices, rising land cost will eventually push up BTO prices in the long run.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In addition, the long waiting time of BTO flats has caused many young couples to choose to buy flats at high prices in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The current high property prices are not only a heavy burden to many young people, but also a shackle that keeps them from starting a family and developing their talents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is only when they sell the flat that they need to return the land cost together with interests to the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This means that if a couple lives in the same flat from the time they get married to the end of their life, they do not have to pay the land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These two policies will significantly reduce the housing burden of young people, give them more space to start their own businesses and fulfil their dreams, and inject new vitality into the city.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: More importantly, with reduced housing costs, young people do not have to use a large portion of their CPF savings to service their housing loans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This will break the vicious circle of "house prices must continue to rise, otherwise Singaporeans will not have the money to retire".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP is of the view that Singaporeans should not need to sell their flat or lease for old age, and that everyone should own a flat while meeting the Basic Retirement Sum.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Our country has sufficient resources to realise this vision.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This dream can be translated into reality by PSP’s Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Our country can afford the financial expenditure of these policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Singaporeans need not worry too much that our Reserves will be reduced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We will continue to uphold the principle of "planting trees to provide shades for future generations." On the other hand, many senior citizens who own flats with shorter and shorter leases have another worry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Many Singaporeans use their CPF savings to service their housing loans, so they have to find ways to monetise their flat after retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: HDB flats are one of our greatest achievements, but HDB housing policies must stay relevant to ensure that every generation of Singaporeans can benefit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Our land is a precious asset, shared among each generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP’s Affordable Homes Scheme will be a wise and sound way to ensure that Singaporeans can benefit from our land assets for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is also in line with, and a continuation of the spirit of land reform that the Government has been carrying out under the Land Acquisition Act for nearly half a century.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the President said at the opening of this 14th Parliament that Singaporeans are masters of their own land.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But that rings hollow when a significant number of Singaporeans have difficulties owning a house.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have spoken about this in my maiden Parliamentary speech on 1 September 2020.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I said, "it is disconcerting to have many of countrymen live outside Singapore in Johor and Batam while we are housing more than two million foreigners on our island at the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Surely more consideration can be given to Singaporeans who are citizens of our sovereign city state." So, let us work together as one united people to achieve a better future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we do not want to prolong the debate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I just want to make sure that we put that on record.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Thirdly, Mr Speaker, I thought that we should settle this before we start voting on both Motions and the Workers' Party's amendment of our Motion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In deciding how to vote on each Motion, including PSP's Motion, I invite the Members of the Workers' Party or the Leader of the Opposition to spell out clearly your position or the Workers' Party's position on PSP's Motion as well as on the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I intended to put some clarifications to the Minister and also address that point which Minister requested for earlier with regard to WP's position on the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Our view is that it is an intriguing proposal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Our own view is that it should be studied further.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is the same for their Millennial Apartments Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the point about our view on PSP's Motion, I believe I already covered it in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first clarification I have is with regard to his point that in the course of addressing some of the pain points with housing policy today, the Forward Singapore exercise would be one platform which would be used by HDB and the Government to seek feedback from Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In this vein, I refer to the report of the Land Working Group of the Economic Review Committee (ERC) in 2003, which I referenced in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: When that report was released, industry watchers opined that the Land Working Group could not undertake a proper review of land policy because public housing was not within the committee's purview and neither was HDB or MND actually represented on the Land Working Group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As part of the Forward Singapore exercise, would the Minister consider standing up a committee to look into the impact of growing land prices and increasing taxpayer subsidies on HDB affordability in particular?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second query I have is with regard to the Minister's handout, specifically Annex 5.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the Minister have a view on the reasons for the steep demand from second-timers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand earlier he mentioned demand was broad-based, but does the Minister believe that the creeping reality of lease decay is also a driver behind this steep rise?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it was 140% over the time period that was identified in Annex 5.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I made some reference to the POFMA Order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am sure the POFMA Order was drafted very carefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Point number six of the POFMA Order I referred to, the one of 14 October, said that the Government cannot sell state land at nominal or much lower cost than its fair market value.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I was inquiring in my speech whether HDB priced land with some different valuation or modelling in mind vis-a-vis public housing because it says not at a much lower cost.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, really, what are we referring to here?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that really focuses on the questions that I have been asking and the detail that I have been seeking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister replied about and I think I have heard him more than once refer to the brochure, and he uses this word repeatedly – "broadly reflects", "broadly reflects", "broadly reflects".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Hence, my clarification and my use of Waterway Banks, which was employed by the Minister for National Development in 2013 in his Parliamentary reply, where he could identify specifically subsidies, the fixed costs, and he identified the figure without a problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not believe HDB does that and I believe it can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, I think I have addressed the question that the Minister raised about WP's position on PSP's proposals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I welcome the Leader of the Opposition's clarification that Workers' Party does not support PSP's proposals on the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Whichever way it votes on the Motion later, I think that clarity is helpful for the record and to understand the Workers' Party's position on affordability, accessibility and the proposed reset by PSP.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the 2003 ERC report, I do not have the report with me at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will have to go back and view that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would just say this – that as part of Forward Singapore, we have already embarked on a number of conversations with people from across different walks of life and also received lots of representation by Singaporeans and organisations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, there is another one going on tomorrow night where people would want to share their views about public housing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are many platforms for Singaporeans and well-wishers to contribute their ideas, views, data and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On Annex 5, the Member is asking us to give a sense of why the demand has shot up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the interest of not prolonging the debate, I have covered some of that in the opening speech as to the kind of dynamics and the interplay of factors which led to the spike in demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I think there are, of course, other factors as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For second-timers, they are applying for a variety of reasons – some because they need housing, some because they see the wide gap between resale prices and BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are all views that one can make as to what interplay of reasons led to this market psychology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the POFMA question, let me go back and have it properly addressed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the Member would file a Parliamentary Question, I will have it properly checked because it is a legal matter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And lastly, on subsidies, when I said, "broadly reflects", I wanted to be very accurate because we provide price ranges for each project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, when you see 5-room flats in Central Weave @ AMK, they are 5-room flats on different floors, and therefore, the price before grant is different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The comparable resale prices which is put right next to the BTO prices are again in a range because you have probably a variety of resale transactions around the area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some professional work needs to be done to adjust for tenure, adjust for condition, amenities, and so on, and these are professional matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I wanted to be accurate to say, "broadly reflects" because there are all these considerations will be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am of the opinion that the point about NIRC is a very important one.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can I request the Minister to respond to that point properly?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I really do not want to start the three-day debate right now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is why as an act of kindness to all Members, we have said that we would just register that it is incorrect and we will debate it later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Minister, I would accept that you register that this is an outstanding issue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not accept that this is an inaccurate fact.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Member does not need to accept that it is inaccurate or not so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am stating our position that it is inaccurate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He is free to debate that if he wishes, but that should be done on another occasion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Whilst I am here, Mr Speaker, may I seek a further clarification from the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Earlier on, Minister Desmond Lee had asked the Leader of the Opposition to clarify the Workers' Party's position on the Progress Singapore Party's Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think he asked about the position that Workers' Party has on the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The leader of the Opposition said, if I understood him correctly, that it is an intriguing proposal that needs further study.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That does not actually quite answer the question, but let me put the question more clearly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Motion by the Progress Singapore Party says that this House calls on the Government to review its public housing policies in order to deliver affordable and accessible HDB flats for Singaporeans and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, if what the Workers' Party is saying is that it can vote in favour of the Motion, but not necessarily in favour of the two schemes, then I would be grateful if the Leader of the Opposition could clarify that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, indeed, I thought I had made it clear in my reply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I had also made it clear in my speech what our position was on the Progress Singapore Party Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the operative word, when the People's Action Party Members spoke about the Motion was that they were reading an implication into that Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I had just stated our stand clearly that we do not read it that way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We do not see the Motion per se in an insidious fashion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Insofar as the schemes are concerned, we see them as different from the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the exact words I used in my clarification was, "These are not our proposals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We do feel that they should be studied further." I hope that clarifies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the decision, as I understand it, is that the Workers' Party will vote in favour of the Progress Singapore Party's Motion, but keeps a safe distance from the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennium Rental Scheme.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I just want to clarify with Mr Leong whether he is aware that Singapore's home ownership rate is 89% because I started yesterday by disagreeing with him.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But the more I listened, the more I think it is scary and dangerous, and it is like a gust of Progress Singapore Party wind can blow us all off.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, I appreciate what Mr Leong said about doing more for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I know we want to have more Singaporeans to get onto the property ladder; we can give them a stool to climb up; but he is not doing that; he is taking down the whole ladder.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I just want to make the comment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have now, finally, come to the conclusion of the debate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I shall put the necessary questions to the House for decision.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will first deal with the Motion by the Minister for National Development on Affordable and Accessible Public Housing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have a substantive amendment by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh's amendment is in line 4 of Minister Lee's Motion to delete the words "endorses the commitment of the Government to" and to replace them with" calls on the Government to intensify its efforts to meet".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will deal with the amendment by Mr Pritam Singh first.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is, "That this House affirms the importance of keeping public housing affordable and accessible while protecting the interests of current and future generations of Singaporeans, and endorses the commitment of the Government to these twin goals."

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As many as are of that opinion say "Aye".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would you like to record your dissent, or would you like to call for a division?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Will hon Members who support the division, please rise in their places?

speaker: Mr Speaker
